title: D&D game Warlock's slick new gameplay trailer looks like BG3 and Control had a baby
content:
A new trailer for the upcoming D&D game Warlock has just dropped at GamesCom's Opening Night Live, promising a more action packed take on the world's first roleplaying game. Practically all of the best DnD games ever made have been RPGs of one class or another, but Warlock is a third person action adventure - and the new trailer reveals it will focus on systems-driven combat that puts me in mind of both Baldur's Gate 3 and, weirdly, Control.

Player character Kaatri is a blademaster who has sealed a pact with the archfey Tasha, agreeing to serve the powerful witch in exchange for a portion of her magical power. The spells she learns from her pact get used inside and out of combat. A telekinetic Mage Hand allows Kaatri to clear obstacles from her path, yeet them at her enemies, or pull them down onto their heads; Misty Step acts as both a combat dodge and a way to pass through grates; and entangling magical vines can both hold platforms for traversal puzzles and tie an enemy in place.

It's always elegant when a game makes the same abilities usable in and out of combat, good for immersion and for muscle memory alike. In combat there seem to be limited charges for each magical power, but outside combat their use looks unlimited. The fact that most powers have a traversal use as well as a combat use also means there's scope for Metroidvania style progression gating, though that hasn't been advertised so far.

There's also an elemental effects system. Close to the start of the trailer, Kaatri clears the vines obstructing a gate by hurling a lantern at it to light it on fire, then dousing it with a bucket of water. Near the end of the trailer Kaatri enacts a short ritual and summons a rainstorm, dousing several bonfires and seemingly rendering a group of zombies more susceptible to a lightning strike attack.

I could pull out any number of comparison points for this kind of gameplay. CRPG gamers will be most familiar with it from Baldur's Gate 3, there are similar ideas in the two most recent Zelda games, and we could point to Bioshock for an example of these attacks showing up in an action game context. Kaatri even uses telekinesis to knock an enemy into a hole at one point, which is basically a kick - if she can stack boxes to break out of the critical path we might be able to call this an immersive sim!

But why does the third person action make me think of Control? Partly it's the aesthetics, like the particle effects that accompany main character Kaatri's dodge, or the way different environments connect together with slightly dreamlike transitions. Partly it's the way her spells mean she and her enemies are only loosely associated with the ground. Mainly, it's the way that Kaatri's nonlethal spells interact with the element system so that the levels themselves become a key resource for harming enemies - or at least, that's what the trailer is trying to sell.

I like what I'm seeing here, but this trailer is a very carefully stage-managed version of the game. The HUD is extremely restrained: there's no targeting reticle, no markers to indicate when you've highlighted an interactable object to use your Mage Hand on. I don't doubt that this trailer came from recording a build of the game, but I don't expect that the actual game to look like this. Nor do I expect that an actual player - without a script of when to show off each ability- to put so much emphasis onto looking cool unless it's also the most efficient way to kill every enemy on screen. A real player might use mage hand to pull a pillar onto a cultist's head once to see what happens, but 99% of players won't do it more than once unless it can trigger really goofy ragdolls.

While the trailer is staged, that doesn't mean the finished game won't contain all these elements; I just don't expect the reality of playing with them to be so slick. And the sales pitch is a strong one: who doesn't want to swing a sword and sling spells? Particularly with Lady Dimitrescu's voice actor Maggie Robertson giving you instructions.

What do you think? Is this promising, or are you sceptical of just how slick it looks? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Turn Order: Paper Minis for TTRPGs - The Artists and Creators
content:
What Are Paper Minis?

Paper Miniatures sometimes also known as “standees” are an old school form of TTRPG miniature. The ones I’m talking about are perhaps even simpler than some of the really old ones that predate inkjet printing by a few decades. There are videos out on the internet of Peter Cushing (yes Tarkin) painting toy soldiers made of compressed drawing paper. What I’m writing about today is a bit more modern than that though I promise.

Selection of Paper Minis from PrintableHereos.com and PaperForgeMinis.com

What Advantages and Disadvantages Do They Have?

Paper Miniatures are cheap and quick to make in large numbers to a high level of quality. If your party is facing a horde of Goblins or Kobolds next week getting said horde printed and ready is something doable in a single day from start to finish. I know this website has plenty of people that love to paint miniatures but when you’re trying to run a sandbox as a GM being able to react to the players between sessions is something I value highly, and these minis look better than any goblin army I’d paint in a week or two (heck even in a month).

They have some of the same downsides as plastic or resin minis (bought or printed) though, some of them avoidable. For instance I tend to print my own minis with their bases attached, folding them into the required shape. The space required to store minis like this is something Warhammer playing readers of this website are probably all too aware of. Many paper mini users instead print their minis flat and use slot bases to stand them up for us, letting the mini itself be stored flat in something like a TCG Binder. To save space and to fit larger maps into a smaller amount of table space I actually print my minis at 15mm scale (more on that later) a size that slot bases aren’t sold at. I also use a monitor to display maps on in my games so I’m perhaps a bit overly cautious about the impact of a plastic base on the screen’s surface over time. It might be a simplistic understanding of materials science but “harder material wins” is the level I understand and I want the winning material to be the screen not my minis. The big disadvantage though you can only avoid so much with them is that they are still made or paper (or card) and therefore not going to outlast a plastic mini with regular use. In my experience I’ve gotten several years out of my players' minis without needing to replace them though, with careful use and storage I wouldn’t call them fragile.

Size though I think is an advantage I’m surprised I don’t see talked about more by 3D printing TTRPG players. There are lots of minis you can buy for games like D&D, but they’re almost exclusively at the 28mm scale. Maybe the UK dining table is just a bit smaller than the average but fitting character sheets, dice trays, note books, and a decently sized map on the table at that scale quickly presented itself as one of the first challenges I faced as a new GM a few years ago.

Early Days of GMing - Credit Vre’kais

Roughly 20 x 8 squares and I’ve almost crossed the entire width of my table at the usual 1” grid scale. I really wanted to fit a more meaningful amount of space on my table and it occurred to me that I could make my minis any size I want.

Paper minis on a screen showing a VTT Map - Credit Vrekais

This 18.5” portable screen fits a 27 x 15 15mm grid in less space than two pieces of A4 paper.

One last big advantage I’ve found of Paper Minis is how easy they can be to adjust or edit if the exact mini you need doesn’t exist yet. You might not have even realised it but you’ve seen one already in this article!

Modified mini created using minis from PrintableHeroes.com

This Tent Mimic is actually a Tent mini crossed with a barrel Mimic’s teeth and tongue, with a smattering of eyes for good measure.

What Providers Are There?

I won’t even pretend that this list is exhaustive, it’s not even close, but they’re the creators I’ve used the most as well as some I’m aware of with different styles.

Printable Heroes & Paper Forge

Printable Heroes and Paper Forge are probably my first go for 99%+ of my mini needs, with a catalogue that as their names suggests doesn’t just cover monsters, there’s a vast array of player character art in here to choose from as well. What I really like about these two though is how compatible their styles are when used together. To some extent they’ve also tended to not overlap on more niche things if the other has one already which is a breath of fresh air in this competitive world we live in. They both also have some of the most helpful and friendly discord communities I’ve joined. Here’s a bunch of player characters I printed and whilst I think most people might be able to figure out which is which given enough scrutiny it’s not jarring enough to be an issue.

Paper minis designed by PrintableHeroes.com and PaperForgeMinis.com, printed by Vre'Kais

Both of these creators offer a large selection of mini art for free with variants and some very specific minis being only available to subscribers of their respective Patreons. Considering both have offerings starting as low as $1/month though neither are especially expensive and both put out minis at a decent rate usually several per month on average.

Paper minis designed by PrintableHeroes.com and PaperForgeMinis.com, printed by Vre'Kais

PrintableHeroes current long term goal is to try to cover the entire D&D monster manual but the latest release on their website was No.1174 and there’s only roughly 300 monsters in that book so some side quests have certainly been taken on their way to achieving that goal. Between these two providers though I’ve very rarely not been able to find something I need or that I can uses as a proxy.

There's also a great community for modifying the minis using parts of other minis. For instance I’m running a campaign of Curse of Strahd Reloaded currently and reached out for help finding a reasonable proxy for “The Strix” a large bird construct with Manticore stats and abilities. Someone in the Printable Heroes discord actually “kit bashed” me something that was almost perfect using parts of several different minis combined into something new.

Uses Paper minis designed by PrintableHeroes.com and combined by CapZylo

Hero Forge

Sometimes though I have to admit that these providers can’t provide for every single character fantasy, so for those I’ve turned to using exports from Hero Forge. There’s a few different approaches you can take here though, I’ve tried both doing front and back images separately and lining them up as close as I can, but also more recently accepted defeat and mirrored a single image front and back. Perspective on a 3D model causes the size of elements from each view to vary quite considerably. When I was still cutting minis out by hand this wasn’t a big issue but since swapping to a digital cutter those differences are very difficult to work around.

Selection of Paper Minis including some using Hero Forge exports - photo by VreKais

I’ve also resorted to combining art from Hero Forge and Printable Heroes when necessary, a combination that worked far better than I actually ever expected considering the very different styles. In this case it was needing a PC mini for both mounted and unmounted combat, as their Drake beast companion was a key part of the character’s identity that I definitely wanted to see on the table.

Combination of Hero Forge mini and PrintableHeroes.com art, photo by Vrekais.

To create this I actually posed the character mini in Hero Forge on a motorcycle, and then edited that out of the image to pose him on top of the Drake.

Other Artists

I’ve covered the art providers I’ve used but there are loads more I’ve seen and want to make sure I mentioned a few of them here.

Trash Mob Minis

Credit Trashmob Minis Patreon

An incrementally more cartoony style than Printable Heroes and Paperforge, these minis certainly have a lot of charm with bright bold primary colours and distinctive designs. They're probably the first provider I’d recommend for games aimed at a younger audience.

Paper Mage

Credit Paper Mage Patreon

At the other end of the illustrated style spectrum Paper Mage has a few hundred designs available. I haven’t used them myself but they are highly recommended in the paper miniatures communities I frequent.

This barely scratches the surface of the creators out there designing mini art for almost any vibe or setting now. I’ve asked around the communities I’m in for more suggestions and here’s a quick list of those recommendations.

  • David Okum (Okumarts)
  • Yasashii Kyojin Studio
  • Lichfest
  • PaperMini
  • Kev's Lounge
  • HUMAN PERSON

I’ve had a great time enhancing my games with these amazing artists' help over the last few years and I hope this quick tour of what’s available inspires more people to give them a try! I’ll be back soon with a guide on how I print, cut, and prepare my minis soon!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: The new Cosmere board game is a 3 hour fantasy world war, with some promising twists
content:
Of all the board games, wargames, card games, and RPGs I checked out at Gen Con 2026 (in between meetings, atrocious burritos, and cowering in fear of tornadoes) my preview of War for Roshar, with its designer John D Clair, was among the more surprising highlights. Why should I be surprised to be excited about Brotherwise's third and latest Brandon Sanderson board game, you ask?

A fair question. After all, the last two (a Sanderson reskin of the O'Neal brothers' hero-creating game Call to Adventure in 2020, then Clair's own Mistborn Deck-building Game in 2024) were both well received. The Cosmere TTRPG raised over $15 million from backers in 2024, making it the most successful tabletop Kickstarter ever (until Avantris' $16m Neon Odyssey unseated it this year). And, while reviewers - including our own Mollie Russell - found the Cosmere RPG somewhat hidebound by its own complexity, its deep, beefy systems, paired with Sanderson's enormous lore base, have generally impressed.

Why, then, should I not already have been foaming at the mouth for another tabletop entry, especially one in a genre I'm particularly partial to: massive dudes-on-a-map strategy games with generous dollops of politics added? It's time I admitted it: I am an almost total outsider to the works of Brandon Sanderson. My experience of his Cosmere fantasy universe amounts to reading literally the first couple chapters of Mistborn book one (the first of seven) and bouncing off, ungripped. If you're the sort of fan for whom that instantly disqualifies me from having opinions on any related topic, you may go now in peace, with my blessing.

If you're still here, though, let's dig into what I learned from chatting to War of Roshar's designer John D Clair that piqued my interest more than Sanderson managed to. First off, a bird's eye view of the basics: this game is set on the planet Roshar, the setting of Bran-San's other epic fantasy series The Stormlight Archive.

These stories take place on Roshar's single, Pangaea-like supercontinent, which was devastated by an empire-shattering war of godlings 4,500 years ago and is now constantly fought over by two dozen rival nations, with varying levels of moral depravity. All are seeking out powerful magic macguffins that'll give them the upper hand, but they're kept in deadlock, largely because (and here's the classic Bran-San twist card) gigantic, destructive magical storms ravage the entire continent once a week.

Even to my non-Sanderson-pilled mind, that is a potent recipe for a dudes-on-a-map strategy game, with plentiful opportunities for the lore-backed mechanical kickers such games need, to stop them descending into 'basically just Risk'. Loads of competing successor kingdoms? Sounds like we could be bartering alliances and levying troops to our coalition! Legendary magical artefacts that could turn the tides of war? Oh mamma, I'll fight pyrrhic battles to nab those! World spanning storms? I bet those could provide random environmental threats that'll menace factions large and small!

Well, as Clair tells me, the game has all those elements. For one thing, those sentient 'highstorms' rack both sides in random areas of the board every round, stopping either player from resting on their laurels too long. For another, the titular war is the one against the rage-god Odium that ramps up across the second and third Stormlight books. Key plotlines from those novels - raising a military coalition against Odium, and securing the magical, army-teleporting Oathgates - do indeed form the bones of this board game. We'll get to all that.

But the leading feature, the one Clair seems most enamored with, is even more narrative focused: it's the people. All your favorite book characters are here, and they're baked right into the heart of the game. "I call it a hero-driven game," he says, "because all of the actions you take during the game are done by heroes, and then the troops that they command.

"So if I activate a particular hero, that hero can move, and then he or she can do a command action based on [what's around them], and those are the troops that you can move. So you're all driven by where your heroes are and able to influence the board." For all the Stormlight Archive books' big, board-gamey war-drama, many fans' favorite bit is its massive, diverse cast of characters - each with different origins, attributes, and viewpoints on the world's woes. So Clair, who introduces himself to me right up top as an enthusiastic Cosmere fan, has made a point of placing the novels' beloved big names at the forefront of War for Roshar's gameplay.

"Crucially," he explains, "each player actually gets two heroes, and the pairing of your two heroes is where a lot of the strategy and implications come in". Our demo setup at Gen Con showed a player set up with Kaladin and Jasnah. "But in a different game," says Clair, "we might have Shallan and somebody else. And it's the same for Odium factions - they're gonna have different heroes playing them".

Each hero, Clair says, is "quite asymmetric in two ways". Through the game, you'll be removing cubes from the player board housing your two hero cards, which "reveals either more strength to the hero or one-time powers that they can do" - but also unlocks Radiant Powers the heroes can activate for boons in and out of battle.

Beyond that RPG-esque 'leveling up', though, your choice of leaders also determines your strongest opening moves, Clair tells me. "Every hero has two starting cards they start with. Hero actions are, for the most part, driven by playing cards… and the two cards your heroes start with matter."

In fact, card play drives every action in the game, because - unlike the archetypal map-control strategy games of yore - there are no dice here. "Battles in the game are deterministic," Clair says (i.e. stronger army wins) except that "players may have cards in their hand that, once a battle has begun, they can play to influence the battle in secret". Some of these cards, he promises, can have a huge impact even in battles where the outcome seems certain. "A lot of the unexpected moments in the game aren't going to come from a random output", he tells me. "They're going to come from a player action that you didn't expect your opponent to do - which is card-driven."

Not even the drawing of cards is entirely random, either. "Some actions you can take in the game let you go through one of your faction's decks and add a new card to your hand, and that card is not revealed to your opponents until you actually play it," Clair reveals, "so a lot of the unexpected stuff is going to come from that". That's also the main way to shape your overall strategy once the game really gets going, it seems. "The choice of characters we got at the beginning matters a lot," Clair explains, because "if I know you have that character, as an experienced player, I know what your strengths and weaknesses are".

"But then, as we play, much of what our ultimate powers end up being are what we draft from the decks as we play. So, though I may start with Kaladin and Jasnah, as I play, I can draft into flexibility to try to counter what your strengths are - and buffer my weaknesses." Carefully upgraded or not, though, the heroes do have some inherent skills and weak points, intended both to balance them in-game, and to anchor them to their counterparts in the novels.

"A character like Jasnah, she's not especially great as a commander on the battlefield, but her diplomacy is amazing," Clair says, whereas "Dalinar, he's a very good commander on the board, and he's a pretty good fighter himself in battles, and his diplomacy is okay, but gets progressively better - fitting his character arc".

Which brings me to a particularly enticing point: battlefield prowess isn't the only skillset you'll need to optimize your hero leaders for; you also need them to make friends and influence people. Winning the war for Roshar depends as much on diplomacy as it does on taking heads - and,  judging by Clair's description, this half of the game appears more satisfyingly integrated than it normally is in this sort of fare. That's mainly because you actually have to do some of it in order to expand.

The basic system isn't complicated: all the board's many nations are represented on an Allegiance Track showing whether Odium or the Coalition is their best friend, and sending one of your heroes to do a Diplomacy Action in a nation's capital brings it closer to your side. What's more impressive to me is how the implications of national allegiance are so neatly blended into the core wargame, as opposed to merely imposing boring, transactional buffs and debuffs around the edges.

"On the board," Clair eagerly explains, "there are a bunch of neutral nation troops, and they basically just sit in that nation's territory and defend it. If either side moves in, they'll fight them, right?

"But if you pull that nation towards your allegiance, they won't fight you anymore. They'll only fight the other side. And if you pull them all the way - not just Friendly to you, but all the way to Aligned - all those troops actually flip and turn into your troops, and now you can help command them into battles."

"That push and pull matters a lot," he says - "especially when you need to get into nations and you want to be able to recruit new troops there". This topic pricked my ears up, because it's a real sticking point for wargames in general. A common complaint about lightweight war board games is that they can gloss over the vital challenge of maintaining your conquered territory, to maintain supply lines and protect against insurgencies. A common complaint about heavyweight war board games is that they can take up half your time faffing around with supply lines, economy, and other stuffy subsystems, when what you really want to be doing is having a damn good battle. Solving this fiendish tightrope act is a real puzzle for board game designers.

War for Roshar's solution, at the very least, seems to have a basic elegance and verisimilitude. Essentially, diplomacy takes longer but pays off more in the end, while pure conquest moves faster and breaks more stuff, but quickly leaves you overextended and fending off constant insurrections, because conquered peoples don't tend to like it very much. "If I go into a nation hoping I can recruit troops, I have two ways to do it," Clair explains. "One, make them friendly, and now I can recruit troops for them. Or two, outright conquer them and then recruit troops."

"But if I conquer them, they're going to fight back," he says. "Each round we flip a card that spawns new neutral troops in various nations. So if I'm trying to repress a nation so I can recruit there, throughout the game they're gonna gradually be spawning new troops that keep fighting back a little bit." There's a touch of faction asymmetry here too, as Odium is most often better at aggressive conquest, and the Coalition "has a bit more ability to control and less ability to conquer" - though Clair assures me both can win either way.

One final design twist takes us even further away from bog standard Risk-alikes, and that's the victory condition: the ten magical Oathgates arrayed across the board. Over two to four hours ("we didn't constrain ourselves too much on trying to hit a lighter target and a short time play," says Clair) you're fighting to take and hold as many gates as you can and, crucially, more than your opponent.

Each round, the two sides count up their gates to reach the victory point threshold needed to win, and the side with more gets a VP bonus equal to their lead. It's like the opposite of a catch-up mechanic; it's there to put the loser out of their misery. It's not quite as brutal as it sounds, though, because all Oathgates are not created equal: the factions take turns to assign a VP value of 0-3 to each gate, effectively betting on the ones they're most confident they can take and hold.

By my lights, this all adds up to a very appealing, cohesive layer cake of strategy mechanics, with asymmetry peppered judiciously throughout, rather than concentrated in just the faction system, as is more usual. Armies operating as functions of your named heroes - and their battlefield success being a mixture of pure numbers and the sneaky actions of those heroes - is a neat way to keep Sanderson's famous characters center stage. Baking the diplomatic challenge directly into the same strategic decision space used for your war plans makes it crunchy and relevant, without clogging up a midweight wargame with administrative jetsam.

Will those ingredients coalesce into a strategy board game I'll actually want to keep playing for a 4 hour session (which is undoubtedly the minimum my first few games will take)? I'll have to wait until it's in my hands to find out. Brotherwise is launching War for Roshar on Kickstarter on October 13, at which point we'll also find out how much they're charging for this long-haul fantasy bunfight.

If you're a Sanderson and/or Stormlight fan who didn't click off when I said I hadn't read the books, come join the free Wargamer Discord and let me know if you're jazzed for this game - I'm genuinely interested in the perspective of folks whose interest, unlike mine, is as much for the lore as for the gameplay!

title: Malediction: Monofaction Reinforcement Packs
content:
New releases for the miniature card game Malediction are on the horizon, and no matter which faction or seeker you play, there is something for everyone. The new faction packs bring new units, spells, and items for you to utilise for your expedition into the Malediction. Let’s peek behind the curtain and take a look!

The Four Reinforcement Packs for Malediction - Loot Studios

What Are These Packs?

These new sets are Reinforcement Packs that focus on a specific monofaction with the game. They have fixed contents and are not boosters, so nothing is randomised within them. Each focuses on a specific aspect and playstyle of a faction, expanding your tools for the tabletop. There are 3x Units, 3x Spells, and an Item in each set, alongside the STLs for you to print the models. If you’re not a fan of printing the models, then you can pick up the standee pack that will be coming out with the Reinforcement Packs, allowing you to play with the cards straightaway. 

Hands of the Church Miniatures - Loot Studios

Hands of the Church - Order of the Shattered Throne

Sacrifice for the greater good is the core concept of this set. We are finally diving into what makes The Church of the Order’s lands tick; powerful effects that have a dire cost.

Units

Siro, Hand of Law - Gaining echo is likely one of the strongest effects in the game considering how premium of a resource it is. The Pray ability from the Valcarist Priests have been used by the Order to help generate more echo for the player to spend, and here you can do so through a similar ability as a trade for damage, which can be so easily healed since you are playing the faction that heals but also prevents damage. 

But you can couple this with doing more damage using the echo you just gained. Turning Siro into a little bit of a beast. But the true power lies in using him with Sigrith. Her Legacy allows you to discard cards to prevent damage, as well as allowing you to make a free attack if you fully prevent the damage. Siro can force free attacks with his abilities, whilst also generating more echo. 

Sigrith and Siro will be an incredible duo, imposing an incredibly tough control on the board. You just have to get Siro out of your deck and onto the field as soon as possible. 

Gilded Sentries - The sentries are beasts! They can charge an enemy model if it has made an attack on a friendly, and with their base 5 damage on a hit, they will mess you up. It isn’t often you see such a high damage on a non-Seeker model, so it makes these standout. They’re also pretty tough to take down with 14 defence and health. Will be in my decks going forward for sure!

I also like the idea that this can work well with a “fights back” deck. You could have the Armoured Revenant be the front line with the Gilded Sentries being nearby. If the Armoured Revenant is attacked, it will fight back, followed by the charge from the sentry. Then, the enemy needs to get through the sentry which is no easy feet. 

Discordant Voice - What a crazy cheap unit to add to the game, but its playstyle around control is brilliant. The best way to understand these units is by treating them as traps. They do damage when an engaged enemy activates, and you can set them up when your own units activate. Having these work alongside the Revalis Penitent would mean when an enemy model activates it would take 3 damage. 

I love the idea of throwing these annoyances into opponents who will either need to kill the model, or spend their activation getting away from them. You can delay the most important models on the table with such cheap troops. Love these as an addition to the Order’s roster. 

Spells

Triumvirate Liturgy - This spell is a really useful card since it is technically free as long as you have five echo to spend to play it, since you can get it back from the effects. Drawing some more cards to help get through your deck or refreshing an ally is incredible value. But, the trade off for it being for free, would be giving an effect to your opponent. 

You can get around it by playing it in a round in which you would go first, and then drawing two cards whilst refunding your spent echo. Your opponent can then refresh an ally, but no one would have been exhausted to refresh. But, refreshing yourself in the direst of moments, could be a powerful play. The versatility is what excites me about this card. 

Demand Confession - This spell is not that impactful, but it could be a very good card for players in the competitive scene. This is because those at the top of their game would need to have knowledge of most of the cards your opponent could have, whilst also needing to know which ones in a specific moment could do the most harm, thus gaining the most value from this card. 

However, if you have a high cost card in your hand, you could use this to thin the hand of the opponent. It would be very unlikely for them to have an 8 or 9 cost card for example. What you would have to weigh up is whether spending two echo to remove one of your opponents cards is worth it over using the echo to block damage or get a unit out. Unsure on whether we will see this card that often. 

Twisted Clarity - This spell could end up being one of the strongest in the whole pack, perhaps even the game. Being able to fully restore the health of a model can turn the entire tides of a combat by undoing the hard work of the opponent. It is a classical Order style of play, who thrive on controlling the battlefield.

A perfect place to use this card would be in a Londriel Spellwarden deck. Londriel decks that bring the damage-preventing spells of the Order, with the immovable constructs of the Conclave, can be one of the hardest nuts to crack. Now imagine you poured all your resources into weakening the wall you face, and she just plays Twisted Clarity, undoing all you have done. Of course this would mean the model would lose its turn but often it is there to be shield.

It is also a great way to pull your vanguard models out of a bad situation, since they are likely to already be exhausted, whilst taking the main bulk of the damage. I can see this being used on Rogarth or Ephr since you only have one in your deck and they are tanky models for Order. A very good card that will find its way into all of my Order decks. 

Item

Expatrine Scourge - This is utterly incredible. I have not been overly impressed by items in the game; they haven’t provided enough excitement for me to care about them being used. But this scourge changes that. Taking damage to do damage doesn’t seem that incredible on the surface, but with Sigrith you can get extra attacks if you prevent the damage.

Epher, from the Griza Seeker Deck, can do two attacks for one action, each one could take damage through the scourge, allowing you to block the damage on each. You could end up doing eight attacks in one activation with Epher. With half of those attacks doing seven damage on a hit, and all with a range of 3”.

Overall, this set was made with Sigirth players in mind. All the cards have possible places with other Seekers, but their value rockets when brought alongside Sigrith. I expect to be very concerned playing across from Sigirth players going forward, not knowing how many counter attacks could be launched. If you love the paladin of order, then pick this set up as soon as possible. 

Coutly Spectacle Miniatures - Loot Studios

Courtly Spectacle - Legion of the Fallen

Dirty tactics, and cruel debuffs. The Legion rolls out the red carpet for the despicable machinations they have conjured. 

Units

Champion of Drav - This unit is menacing! It reminds me of Strong Belwas from A Song of Ice and Fire with how it encourages an opponent to strike it before striking back, thus allowing them a shot before it demolishes them. Drav wants to get struck in and do some damage, which seems to be low for nine echo, but the Feign Opening rule has a way to increase the damage. If you can find other ways to increase this, then Drav will be a big problem. If I see Drav get played, all my attention will suddenly turn to dealing with it. Very strong and cool model.  

Marsarin Deathsinger - Legion are all about debuffs, and have a few ways to make decisions costly for the opponent. The Deathsinger has a cruel ability which can force the opponent to lose echo if they miss their attacks. Literally rubbing salt in the wound! Again this is another model that I will be gunning for as soon as it hits the table because you can not allow such a leech to remain. You can combine it with a Disciple who can siphon echo from the opponent as well, resulting in a drought of resources. 

Mashr - Most of the lower quality units in the game are not impressive unless they are brought in large numbers. Furthermore, they all fill similar roles of being bodies for the fight more so than anything substantial. The Mashr is actually useful, and I can see them being in every deck going forward. They are there to die so that you can bring on other low quality models such as a Men-at-Arms, but for less echo. They are an investment, and will be a nuisance until they die. 

Spells

Choice of Malady - A cursed decision. Does the opponent exhaust a unit that could be crucial for the turn ahead, all in the aim of preventing more cards drawn? It can be a difficult choice for sure and I am not too sure it is as clean cut of an answer. The power of this card lies in choosing the right moment to play the card. Nothing too crazy with this one. 

Soul Mimicry - Those who have played against Morida know how strong her abilities are when she starts stitching together the abilities of units into an abomination. This spell is like a mini version of that, and can have a massive impact in the game. Grabbing Onslaught and Regeneration from Vorendal as an example, or Morida’s Necromancy action. Normally with these spells they would state “a non-Seeker ally”, but this doesn’t and it can cause a world of pain. Very good card indeed. 

Horrific Archery - A brilliant card that works perfectly with Vorendal’s Legacy, so this will certainly be used with his forces. However, the ranged buff part of this card is a really good effect as there are not many things available to the Legion that has ranged. You could pair it with a model that has the Ambush rule, and wants to attack a target but can’t due to terrain or models. This card is a great utility piece for the Legion. 

Item

Oskarite Blade - This item is incredible, and I can see all factions looking to play it. A passive buff to damage, whilst also offering more scoring points for the game. This is worthwhile in all decks and for use on all capable units. There are some like Ephr from the Order roster, that can do multiple attacks against targets, that would be the best place for this attachment as an example. One of the best attachments in the game. 

This is a brilliant set for all Legion players, and I can see quite a few cards falling into the builds of many decks. Drav is the coolest model created to date, and their rules are full of flavour and awe. I love some of the spells, and I am shocked with how useful the attachments are. If you’re a Legion player, do not miss a chance to grab this set. 

Liastrum Research Miniatures - Loot Studios

Liastrum Research - Conclave of the Spheres

Spells and ranged attacks are the life blood of the Conclave faction, this pack tursn it up to 11.

Units

Athan, Prime Decimator - Athan’s special action can turn his ranged attack into the longest ranged attack in the game that does a whopping ten damage on a hit, and seven damage on a miss. He also suffers damage each time he attacks, whilst also being flung back by the power of his weapon. I can see a few moments where you would take two attacks to blast him 8” away from danger, which is hilarious. Athan is very deadly, and it will be hard to pin him down whilst he snipes your units. 

Thaumite Mercenary - This unit is nothing special in the early game, but will be one of the best fighters towards the middle to end game. Polinore and Londriel burn through spells quite often, so the Arcan Precision ability will be insanely good the longer the game goes on for. But you should equip this model with some damage bonuses from attachments such as the Oskarite Blade from the Legion set we just talked about. You will see these cheap troops become deadly assassins if you’re not careful. 

Liastrum Accumulator - If you couldn’t get your spells out due to shortages of echo, then look no further than the Accumulators. This will be a very strong model to get out on the field as soon as possible. Conclaves thrive on playing spells to buff their forces, so finding ways to make them cheaper is key to keeping the pressure on the enemy. Whilst they aren’t going to be doing much more than counting the pennies of Liastrum, they will become a common occurrence on the battlefield. 

Spells

Liastrum Decimation - What a well designed card. You choose how much echo you would like to spend, based on how much damage you need. There is a discount on some more damage if you buy in bulk. Jokes aside, this is an incredible card. The versatility is incredible, and I can imagine some troll who spends no echo and kills Thundersteps turn 1. A very powerful card that feels like a perfect swiss army knife for almost any situation you may find yourself in. Every deck will surely have this spell included. 

Crackling Trap - Name a more iconic duo than the Conclave and damage dealing spells. This spell adds to the long list of spells in the arsenal of the Conclave that does damage to the opponent, albeit with a little bit more of a restriction. However, everyone should be charging towards Husks as they win the game, so there should be ample opportunities to trigger this card. More damage through spells is music to Conclave ears. 

Salvage - What an interesting card, and one I can see coming into play with a few different units. Reckless Researchers to exhaust the enemy, Virtahn Battlecasters to assail the opponent, and Akheenzan Shieldmages to defend your forces. These elite units are tough to get out, but are even tough to keep around, so pulling them back is incredibly useful. I don’t think this is a card that will have a lot of impact, but in the odd times where it really counts, it can be a life saver. 

Item

Myrkosian Magnifier - This attachment is decent, and has a lot of play no matter which faction brings it. Conclaves are going to see the most value as they should be the ones that go through a lot of spells, but I can also see Sigrith players, or Thundersteps players bringing this card. There is potential in this card in making a unit consistent in combat and there are quite a few models in the game you wouldn’t want to take many attacks from. 

This set comes with added cards that continue the theme for the Conclave, with more ranged attacks and spells that do damage. The highlight will be the Accumulator, which will help you manage your resources far better with how many spells you will be likely using. Athan is a super addition, and I look forward to hearing stories about this sniper on the table. If you love what the Conclave are about, then this is right up your alley. 

Bestial Advantage Miniatures - Loot Studios

Bestial Advantage - Primal Blood

Bestial Advantage focuses on expanding tools around movement to control the battlefield, whilst unleashing plenty of pressure from swarming beasts. 

Units

Irynia and Aratan - This unit allows for fast play with it granting extra movement actions to itself using Dash, and other beasts using Command Beast. Primal Blood are a very fast faction, so adding more of this could make them impossible to catch, or run from. But these abilities work nicely with Swarm, which needs nearby friendlies to gain bonuses to damage. 

The only problem with Irynia and Aratan, is that there are few beasts in the game. I would be using it on the Cursehost Boar for a better position for when it dies and explodes. Or on the Bloodfeast Raptor since it does damage when an enemy activates whilst engaged. More beats are needed, so let’s take a look at them. 

Behemoth Khuyakine - There is no stopping a Behemoth from reaching its prey. I look at the rules for this model and imagine it more like an assassin, getting to far spots to pick off models that believe they are safe behind the frontline. Being able to redeploy can cause a lot of problems for someone trying to control the board. It is also a damaged dealer with five damage on a hit, whilst also being tough to kill with the Resistance ability. A solid model to add to the Primal Blood roster.  

Murder of Shriekers - Another unit that meddles with movement restrictions by swarming through targets doing some chip damage. Chip damage is an interesting concept I have not thought of diving into, but you can stack them nicely with the beasts available for Primal Blood. There isn’t too much to talk about with this unit, and the Primal Blood units have not been that thrilling. The Behemoth has been the highlight however, and I will for sure be bringing them in my decks. 

Spells

Ymirian Rage - This is an incredible spell. There have been many instances where relics alone can decide an encounter or game. But now you can strip such a strong attachment and force another one onto the model, and do some damage to them on top of that. I can see this being in every single deck going forward as it is an incredible card, especially with how overpowered relics can be. 

Landshift - An interesting card for deciding where a fight will be taking place for a round, but not one that is so powerful that it will be a must include. With the speed the Primal Blood has, it could be very easy to contest any Husk. However, you could move the Husk that is being contested towards friendly models, but the path to the husk is blocked by your own. Forcing the opponent to break through the lines to try and stop you claiming it. I can see this card being great against castling opponents. 

Raptor’s Lift - Did I mention Primal Blood are fast? A cheaper card, that gives a nice boost to movement, whilst also providing Fly to get through obstacles. This is a nice situational card that reinforces the faction theme of speed. Nothing too crazy here so not much to talk about. 

Item

Avakran Flute - Battle Cry is an ability we have seen on a model from the Order faction and on the shamans in the Primal Blood, and it is surprisingly very good. Action manipulation can turn an entire game, so being able to bring this as an attachment which a faction can use is quite nice. With Primal Blood being more of a glass cannon, this can help reinforce some damage before a counter assault. For one echo, the versatility it grants is very good. 

Overall the Primal Blood seem lackluster, but perhaps I don’t see the combinations and synergies the cards have to offer? That being said, there are some cool aspects with the Behemoth relocating, a relic recycle, and plenty more movement. Not too bad of a set to pick up. 

What’s the Verdict?

The concept of focusing on one aspect of the background to these factions in small packs is a genius idea. We get to peek into what makes the Church of the Order of the Shattered Throne tick, or how the Primal Blood tame beasts of the land. The rules advance the game in interesting directions, and the miniatures are gorgeous. 

There are competitive pieces, insanely fun aspects, and something for each and every player within these packs. It is a superb release for Malediction that will help freshen the game for those who have been playing for almost a year or longer. I for one cannot wait to paint up some of the models and get them out on the table, with the only question remaining being; which faction should I pick first?

title: eBay clamps down on stolen Pokémon card sales for the 30th Celebration
content:
eBay is reportedly pulling listings that feature cards from the Pokémon TCG's unreleased 30th Celebration set, on the basis that the cards are considered stolen property.

This set, an anniversary celebration marking 30 years of the Pokémon franchise, releases around the world on September 16. But while TPC slowly drip feeds card reveals, the entire set has been widely leaked, and now it seems some of the cards have found their way onto the secondary market ahead of schedule too.

An email, apparently from eBay, was posted to Facebook yesterday by a card seller going by Danny MadTown Collect. It reads:

"The sale of stolen property is not allowed on eBay.

eBay has received communication from The Pokémon Company International indicating that 30th Anniversary Pokémon trading cards are not distributed or made available for public sale through authorized channels as of today. As a result, this listing has been flagged for review.

Based on the information provided by the rights owner, there are concerns regarding the provenance and authorized distribution of this type of item. Specifically, the item may have originated outside of approved manufacturing and distribution processes. To help ensure compliance with eBay policies and intellectual property rights, we recommend that this item not be relisted unless documentation can be provided demonstrating that it was obtained through an authorized and legitimate source."

This came after the seller tried to auction the "first ever" 30th Celebration Sylveon SIR, a full art card from the set.

There are many ways Pokémon cards can escape out into the world before they're supposed to. Leaks can occur at any point in the pipeline: during printing, transportation, storage, or simply by distributors selling the products before they're supposed to. A few years ago there was an incident where, allegedly, a printing worker tried to offload hundreds of stolen rare Pokémon cards from the Fusion Strike set.

This is by no means a problem that's unique to 30th Celebration, but it's obvious that TPC has a particular incentive to make sure things run as smoothly as possible for a Pokémon set that's supposed to be a big birthday celebration for the franchise.

title: Trench Crusade Carcass Front Box Roundtable
content:
It's been a long time coming but the two-player box set for Trench Crusade is finally here. The box includes two new warbands (mostly, we’ll get to that in that section), and two campaigns featuring new scenarios, patrons, and exploration tables, not to mention a ton of cool lore and art that Trench crusade has become famous for. We’ll have articles diving deep into each part of the box, but this is meant to be a roundtable looking at the box as a whole and what we think of it.

Before we dive in, we’d like to thank Factory Fortress Inc for providing us with a preview copy of the rules for review purposes.

New Warbands

Naval Raider Warband Credit: Mildnorman

We have two new warbands: Naval Raiders and Procession of the Sacred Affliction. Both of these warbands were once variant warbands for Heretic Legion and Trench Pilgrims respectively, but are now standalone warbands with their own variants.

Norman: I’m torn on this approach; on one hand, I think expanding on the ideas that were already present in the core factions is a good idea for the game. It means folks will be able to get familiar with like profiles and it gives the designers a good starting point to expound upon. On the other hand, it can feel a bit copy/paste to the point that unless you’re running the War Wolf, there’s not a very compelling reason to go back to Heretic Legion if you’re looking at Naval Raiders. FFI has done a lot of effort to make these Warbands feel distinct but ultimately you can’t unsee their roots. I think a lot of folks are patiently and excitedly (well, maybe not patiently) waiting to see the wacky and weird stuff that hasn’t seen the table yet like Church of Metamorphosis and Path of the Beast, and seeing two factions that we’ve already had a good amount of exposure to might be a bit deflating. That all said, aesthetically, these two warbands are absolutely their own things and have a pretty unique identity so I’m not too beat up about all that.

Dandy: I agree with Norman on the mechanical and rules aspects of the new factions. There’s little to compel me to play a vanilla Trench list or something like Cavalcade, outside of the necessity of a second Punt Gun. Methodius? Sure, that’s distinct enough to get the extra Shrine, but I think that Sacred Affliction offers so much that it kind of overshadows the other Trench Pilgrim warbands. Agreeing with Norman again, the aesthetics are just top-notch. I personally never jived with HNR, but seeing these models and the amazing artwork in the Carcass Front book for the other models just provides such a flavourful take that the narrative and models finally combine to create something really compelling. 

Bre4d: The aesthetics of the factions in the box mesh very nicely together as the “grungy seaside” warbands for the setting of Carcass Front. Not to circle the same point, but these warband variants becoming their own factions do potentially present the problem of making the original versions of them seem bland and not even worth considering when going to play Trench Crusade. On the other hand, as someone who loves to use list building as a way to express myself, it’s great to have more sets of rules within these factions to play around with and try out on the table. 

DGMP: For the most part I agree with the rest of the roundtable about the concern for the new subfactions. Without losing something of significance in choosing to specialize as one of the warband variants, it makes choosing the default option seem either painfully boring or intentionally kneecapping yourself. Why yes I could be normal, or I could take 3 anti-tank hammers on nuns who also get an extra +1 dice to injure downed targets or get +1 Dice to dashing for my entire crew. I love the war wolf, but not that much, I am going +1 Dash and SMG’s for days every time. But simply put, the new warbands are so good it makes me question why you would ever not play as them, unless the vibes for them are just antithetical to your playstyle. However I have faith that in time, Factory Fortress can raise the rest of the rosters up to be just as good, flavorful and fun as these two new ones.

Zaros: I love the idea of fleshing out variants and giving more options, but there is a thin line to walk as everyone has put out. I think for some existing variants, this could be a huge boon for the future but if every variant simply makes the original “variant” overshadowed it doesn’t quite hit the point of intention I believe. Regardless, I will be screaming alongside my triple choristers and grinding my friends to a halt with mass debuffs.

Naval Raiders

You can find our faction focus for Naval Raiders here and the model review here.

Heavy Anointed Naval Raider - @MawQueenMinis

Norman: I love these guys. Are they just Heretic Legion but without the War Wolf and some extra gear? Yes. Does that mean I love them less? Absolutely not. Stuff like the Wrecker’s Torch and Hull Drill will go a long way to making this faction feel a bit more distinct and the lore representation for them (along with the kick ass art) very much makes them feel like they’re their own guys. I do wish they got a Big Guy but I understand why they don’t have one. I do kinda wish that Trench Ghosts had gotten the standalone treatment instead since they have a more distinct roster, but you can’t argue with how good of a fit these guys are for the Carcass Front.

Bre4d: As a Trench Pilgrim simp, I have to say the winners in purely the looks department for Carcass Front would be the Naval Raiders. The Heavy Anointed hit my Bioshock soft spot, and the Chorister with the diving helmet is simply awesome. 

DGMP: Naval Raiders were the faction I played in my first IRL campaign. I am unabashedly biased towards them and I will continue to be so. They are fantastic and I have no plans on dashing less or running less SMG’s in the future with these fantastic models. I am however very excited to try out their new specialties! Leviathan Shoal in particular calls to me, because diving suits are just that awesome. We just need those drill arms now.

Zaros: I touched on it before, but I will scream it out loud again. I LOVE debuff auras. I also love horde focus playstyles (smiles in grunger). The chorister variant offering the best of both is music to my ears, in a very simplified package compared to the infection equation that grunger is. Shoal is going to be insane to see as well, as the ability to give a unit a tough mid match is an insane ability that can swing fights. But my love lies with the choir boys themselves, I shall be chanting to the abyss alongside them…

Sacred Affliction

You can find our faction focus for Sacred Affliction here and the model review here.

Credit: Dandy

Dandy: I was a Sacred Affliction fan when they were in Trench Pilgrims, and that only continues now that they are their own developed faction. From a mechanics perspective, things have stayed the same, with some additions to the Battlekit that further push their offensive power and mobility. I will be interested to see how these additions affect a faction already very strong, as the possibility of wider lists, without sacrificing reliability in mobility/Dashing, kinda fixes one of the few weaknesses the faction had. 

For models, they’re just amazing. Easy to put together, with not just 2 options but also the ability to mix and match them. So it is not just a strict “this or that”, but a chance to make something unique to you. I was initially a little skeptical about the extent to which they could differentiate these models from the vanilla Trench Pilgrims, but they’ve done it! It’s mostly done with bandages. Like, a LOT of bandages, but it's also the hodgepodge nature of the equipment, the religious iconography, and, of course, Millstones. 

Bre4d: Going off of what Dandy mentioned, the ability to mix and match these models is done very well. The fact that FFI was able to do this while the models are as dynamic as they are is super impressive. Although I mentioned that the Naval Raiders eked out a bit better in terms of what I find cool, my favorite shoeless bing bongs were absolutely way easier to build. I still wish we had more Ecclesiastic Prisoner variations, but I guess (literally) beggars can’t be choosers. The aesthetic differences between the original Trench Pilgrims and these sculpts from Carcass Front are a great change, while also being able to fit both kits into the same warband and not have any of them look out of place, which is a huge upside. 

DGMP: The local lepers are sculpted absolutely amazingly. You can practically smell the sickness coming off of every lovingly rendered bandage and boil. And the dad-bod Wrath of God pilgrim! Flawless, no notes. I do share a bit of Dandy’s concern that they really do not seem to have much of a weakness at the moment. Taking Sacred Affliction seems to really be a statement of intent, that intent being that you are going to rush across the board as fast as possible and beat someone's face into the mud like God Himself told you to. Which to be fair is pretty lore accurate. They also have a leg up on the Naval Raiders in the model customization area. The bits for all the various units are generally much easier to swap around and make your own than the Raiders are.

Zaros: I’ll say it one time for everyone in the back; we all LOVE stigmatic nuns. An amazing model with an amazing set of skills and abilities to accompany. The ability to take more of them alongside dope knights with healing capabilities? Sign me up immediately. I still have yet to build a faithful warband yet, and this is my planned first one. I am going to have a blast kitbashing up some leper knights to scour the battlefields!

Campaign Rules

You can find our review of the campaign rules here.

Path to Leviathan

The path to leviathan is a two-player campaign meant to walk new players through the new scenarios. If you’re buying the box as an intro to the game, start here. This guide through the missions is exactly what new players will need and with just 5 games in the campaign. 

Norman: This is a really smart addition from the folks over at FFI. I think a lot of folks are gonna buy this box as a starter set for themselves and maybe a friend and without this would dive into the Carcass Front stuff headfirst and bounce straight off. With this you get a smooth onramp that you can layer as much or as little onto where you can get your bearings.

Dandy: It’s nice to have a structured and easy campaign for beginners to enjoy. Sure, you can start off with simple 700 Ducat games and then move on to one-offs before jumping into a campaign, but getting into a narrative right off the bat is going to be a nice experience for new players. Being able to play this short, scenario-based, narrative campaign as a series of one-offs using the starting warbands lets players jump right into the fun of Trench Crusade. 

DGMP: A perfect weekend campaign to play with whoever you split the box with to cut your teeth on the game system. It’s not only a great introduction to various styles of mission, but it never lets up on the theme and story. It maintains its atmosphere of grungy desperation all the way from scavenging forbidden knowledge to summoning an ancient monstrosity (Almost like a good TTRPG campaign, really) and after those 5 opening games anyone should have a pretty strong grasp of the game and be ready to jump into a new campaign with even more players.

Zaros: Without a doubt, THIS is where new players should start. Diving directly into a proper Carcass Front campaign for a brand new player is going to be extremely overwhelming. This lets them dip their toes properly and prepare themselves for the full plunge when they are properly acclimated and prepared. I think this will create a great transition point for new players; Single Match Play, Path to Leviathan, then a big campaign like Carcass Front.

Carcass Front Campaigns

Sacred Affliction War Priest - bre4d_

The titular Carcass Front Campaign is a broad map campaign that adds node control, resource management, and secret missions to the mix.

Norman: I’m well documented as a Big Fan of narrative game systems. With that in mind, while I like a lot of the things going on here, there’s a lot of stuff. The book does its darndest to make it all digestible, but there’s just a lot of things to keep in your head here between the new exploration tables, the vision cards, and the map itself. I think the ideas here are all good, but you gotta make sure everyone's on board with the extra work going on on top of all the homework associated with post game Trench Crusade (not that that’s too heavy a lift) before you commit to a Carcass Front campaign. I said it above, but thank god for the Path to Leviathan, because without that I think a lot of folks wouldn’t interact with a lot of the systems in here if they tried it right after building their first warband. 

DGMP: I love me some crunchy, complicated rules. And boy, does the Carcass Front deliver lots of those. This is a beefy campaign with a good chunk of new things to keep track of. Secret Missions, a bit of base building, resource gathering, special bonuses conferred by key locations. It’s frankly fantastic but not something you should just spring on a play group without discussing it with them. This will have a bit more of a cognitive load than just rolling up a random mission every week for a few months if that is your current style of campaign. However if your group isn’t averse to adding even more depth to the post game step of Trench Crusade, I think you can get an absolute ton out of this system.

Zaros: As everyone has stated, this is CRUNCHY. There's a lot going on, but I think it is done masterfully for the most part. I love the usage of the map and a new take on exploration. I think that it gives a lot of ideas and inspiration to organizers to really push the limit on campaigns in the future and to not be afraid of diving deep into the nitty gritty. Carcass Front sets a strong precedent of going big, this shows that they are willing and excited to swing wide with interesting and wild concepts that might not hit with everyone. But their presentation and delivery is what sets it up for success. They offer alternatives, designed systems that work independently of one another, and guide organizers and players alike to tailor the campaign experience to what each group is looking for.

Scenarios

Norman: The new scenarios are an interesting one. They’re no doubt cool and thematic, and they avoid the general balance traps you may see when a team goes hard in the paint to tell a story for a scenario. That said, each and every one has either NPC models or bespoke pieces of terrain. These are mitigated through suggestions in the book for replacements and the STLs that are coming if you backed the project, but the main issue is a logistical one. Even if I have all my Mad Monks painted, my Train Gun printed, my piles of scrap drybrushed and my Altar of Leviathan built, it's still an extra thing I’ll need to have on hand if my opponent and I decide to play that scenario. I would’ve liked some more “vanilla” missions but I suppose the random generator accomplishes that goal.

DGMP: I love the visceral feel of these new scenarios. They all have a desperate vibe about them, scavenging things forgotten or thought ruined to try and release an ancient monstrosity. But they all fall into what I consider the “Armored Train” issue. Is the scenario sick? Hell yeah! Does it require its own bespoke special terrain not only to set up but to interact with? Unfortunately also yeah. It is somewhat a cost of having a scenario more interesting and complicated than “Capture the Flag” or “Team Deathmatch” but it is still a barrier to just setting up and playing that I feel needs to be mentioned. As an attempt to smooth this out there are some portions of the rulebook with either paper cutouts you can scan or suggestions it offers to use instead, but the requirement for More Stuff is still there regardless. The new random mission generator is a much simpler addition with no real drawbacks, roll up and set up and you can just get going without any new bespoke shiny things.

Bre4d: The constant struggle of narrative games and the requirement for specific terrain is quite brutal, but once players can get through that barrier of entry these scenarios look like a blast. Not to sound like an online class message board, but I agree with DGMP across the board with how much is required to simply play a game of Trench Crusade, and now Carcass Front has a multitude of additional requirements to get the most out of the game.

Zaros: Adding the need for anything always raises the quote unquote “barrier of entry”, but we also have seen time and time again that the community will always find a way. Kitbashing is at the heart of alternative wargaming, and people have been making their own terrain and models well before Trench Crusade entered the scene. Where there's a want, players will definitely design and print models/terrain to fit the scenarios accordingly aplenty, and I’m certain that it will do the campaign justice. I personally love neutral models that add chaos to the match, and the neutral model rules are excellent! I look forward to the mayhem that will ensue.

Overall Thoughts

Sacred Affliction Ecclesiastic Prisoner - bre4d_

Dandy: All in all, what a box! So two Warbands, some small terrain, as well as tokens, sheets, a brand new narrative book with lore and rules, that can be played with in a dead simple intro game for brand new players, a simple campaign scenario, and then a large map-based campaign mode that introduces mechanics not yet seen? This box has basically something for everyone, regardless of your experience with the game. I’m certainly impressed by how much is crammed in when you stop and think about it.

I think this box is just what the game needed, and those on the fence about jumping in have found the excuse they needed to try it out. As has been pointed out in the campaign section, there’s going to be a lot in the Carcass Front campaign, and it borders on being perhaps a little too much management, but I’m very optimistic about future campaign ideas and what the team can come up with. 

Norman: This is a pretty sick box! There’s a lot to love here, between two new plastic kits (both with amazing sculpts), rules for new warbands, a new campaign system, and a ton of new background lore, there’s some great stuff in here. I’ve got gripes with some things here and there, but for a first big physical release, this is kicking stuff off with a bang. At the end of the day if you’re looking to get into TC, further your TC experience, or just wanna get some cool models, this box is a great buy. I’m really looking forward to seeing what's next from FFI.

DGMP: It is a hell of a box. A solid 8/10 starter box, which I can easily recommend to anyone interested in trying the game who doesn’t want resin minis or Prussians. The new sculpts are fantastic, a perfect blend of being detailed enough to look good without drowning in little greebles just for having as much detail per cubic inch as possible on a model. The token/measuring widget sprue is an amazing little bonus as well, having downed and Tough Removed markers makes things much easier to parse at a glance on the board. Really though I have no complaints, it is a fantastic box for the price point. Sink deeper with the Carcass Front campaign, get started with the Path to Leviathan, it has everything you could want. 

Bre4d: This Carcass Front starter box is a fantastic place for both those who are starting to play Trench Crusade, as well as those who have been neck deep in the game space since the beginning of the TC’s inception. The inclusion of reference materials and ‘how to start’ guides is wonderfully juxtaposed by the gritty and crunchy Carcass Front additions to the base game.  

Zaros: Astounding plastic models and a phenomenal campaign to match, this boxset really hits a homerun and sets a strong baseline of what we expect from Factory Fortress in the future. My excitement for my personal choir knows no bounds and my unending servitude to Charon is cemented (praise be leviathan Master of Death is an insane ability). My local community has been excited for months leading up to the release and our organization of a large scale campaign! I’m excited to see what my talented community comes up with for terrain and model design as well as the rest of the globe and hope the excitement continues to whatever we receive next from the trenches!

title: Trench Crusade Naval Raiders Model Review
content:
With the release of the Carcass Front box comes two new plastic kits for Naval Raiders and Sacred Affliction. Considering these are the second and third plastic releases for TC, this will set the tempo for what we can expect going forward. We'll obviously be starting with the cooler of the two factions (unless you read our Sacred Affliction article first), the Naval Raiders.

Thank you to Factory Fortress Inc for providing us with advance copies for review.

The Build

Most of the models in this kit go together relatively well. If you’re not familiar with Archon’s sprues, they number pieces like you’d expect but also have little arrows pointing to which piece the number refers to, and that's always welcome. All the models stay on their own sprue sheet, but you’ll have to jump around the sheet a bit to find the pieces you’re looking for sometimes.

Each model has an A or B build which can vary from being a completely different looking model, a gun change, or just moving their foot on or off a pipe. Most are the former in that list which is good, but in the instructions we got, it was unclear what pieces were tied to what. For example, Raider 3 can either be built reloading his gun or as a shrouded dual weapon melee guy. The melee weapons on the melee guy can’t be put on the normal body without some careful cutting and greenstuff because the shroud gets in the way. On the flip side, the captain's arms are interchangeable as far as I saw, meaning you can do Shield + Wrecker’s Torch. This can all be figured out with a bit of dry fitting but it’d be nice if in the final instructions it was clearer where the point of no return was.

Now in the initial paragraph you may have noticed I said “most” of the models go together well. The biggest nightmare here is the Chorister. The chain bits all look very similar as bare plastic and it can be really hard to tell what's supposed to connect to what where. I eventually just sorta pressed them all together and they fell into place, but it was a headache for a bit there. In addition, you can’t give him the shark and a shield at the same time, which feels like an attack on me personally considering I’ve never run a chorister without a shield in my life.

There are a few minor gaps on some of these models, with the worst being on the Anointed Heretic Raider, but it’s nothing a bit of pressure, glue and patience can’t solve. All that said, on the whole these models go together without much hassle, I built the whole set in an hour or two after getting the box. You also get a wealth of bits which’ll be going directly into my bits box for future conversions.

MawQueenMinis:  I only had time to build one of the Heavy Anointed, but this model was A LOT OF PIECES. One dude should not be this many pieces, but hey, he looks amazing when he’s together! He was simple compared to the horrors I’ve seen with the Chorister, and I’m not looking forward to building him next. 

Painting

Naval Raider Warband Credit: Mildnorman

My favorite thing about Trench Crusade models is they have just the right amount of bullshit on them. You can sink a ton of time into individual sculpts or get them looking pretty nice and ready in just a few painting sessions (I painted these quickly for the article and got them all done in 2-3 nights of painting). These models are no exception, although some are more annoying than others (it's the Chorister again). 

Not Choristers

For all my normal bozos I followed the same recipe for their armor, going from Games Workshop’s Thunderhawk Blue, washing it with Vallejo Black Wash, and then mixing the original blue with a white to get all my highlights in there. The most annoying part of the model to get done well were by far the lenses. They’re deeply recessed and you want a bright color in there if you want them to be the focal point. I ended up just stabbing Vallejo Troll Orange in there and then white with a smaller brush to try and get in there for some lighting highlights. From there it was just cleaning up with the same armor blue I used everywhere else.

For the cloth, I used Vallejo Bloody Red, washed it down with the same black wash as the armor, and then highlighted with the same color, mixed with Vallejo Grey-White as needed. The cloth provides a nice opportunity to add some uniform color pop to your warband while not being present on every model. This is especially true if you’re doing a raw metal color for the armor like the box art. Same goes with the undersuits, I went with Games Workshop’s Caliban Green highlighted with Vallejo Goblin Green but it's a good place to put some nice contrasting colors.

The Captain was not painted red like the box art because frankly it’d bother me. Instead I put down some Games Workshop Dryad Bark near all the gaps in the armor and went over that with Vallejo Thick Blood to give the suggestion that blood was oozing out of him. Honestly its a hard effect to sell and the model doesn’t really have it modeled on him so you can forgo that little lore blurb entirely if you want.

All in all, these models all have nice dynamic poses that are pretty easy to get a brush anywhere you’d need to with the exception of the captain’s cloak but if you prime black you won't notice the spots you can’t reach. These were fun to paint up and quick which is the most important thing.

Heavy Anointed Naval Raider - @MawQueenMinis

MawQueenMinis: Painting the Anointed may be one of the most satisfying and simple models I’ve painted in a long time. There are just the right amount of unique textures to play with depth, while the flat surfaces are fun to layer up. I went with a layering sponge method for this guy, starting with a black airbrush basecoat. Using Warpaint Fanatic Angel Green, Greenskin, and Ferocious Green I gave him a sponge bath building up each color less and less, taking into account where my light source was. I then edge highlighted a lot of the panels using Ferocious Green. The metals are a simple Vallejo True Metallic Metal Green Gold Base, highlighted with the Light variant, and pinwashed with a watered-down Army Painter Dark Wood. Finally, the tubes are a combination of Pro-Acryl Bright Yellow Green, highlighted with Vallejo Game Color Bile Green. 

I have so much fun basing Trench Crusade models, and this guy was no exception. Wet blending various oranges and throwing a layer of UV resin on top was a really solid way to integrate the model’s base! 

Chorister

Drowned Chorister Credit: MildNorman

This guy… less so. Okay, he’s not that bad, but he is way more annoying than the other models in this set. The chains overlapping the skin in the way they do means you’ll be doing a lot of back and forth between the two materials as you fix mistakes and make highlights. The best method I found was to paint the skin first, then the chains, then the fish, then go back and do it all over again to fix your mistakes. The helmet is mercifully one solid texture outside the porthole so that part is easy enough. The Chorister is also a bit of an odd duck; he doesn’t have the armor or cloth the rest of the warband does so visually there’s very little connecting him to the rest of the force. I elected to paint the big weights on the model’s chest the same color as the armor to add at least a little visual similarity to the other models.

STLs

Leviathal Chorus Credit: Mildnorman

But that's not all! FFI sent us the STLs for the Leviathal Chorus, the Leader for the Chorister warband variant. The model is separated in three pieces and the supports come off relatively easily. If you’re not stupid like me, they’re in pieces that are pretty natural sub assemblies for painting. If you are stupid like me and just put the model together because you got excited, you have a bit of a challenge ahead of you. The base flows into the model and the model’s middle section is a texture nightmare with the choral, intestines, and fish all overlapping each other. I did the same thing I did with the normal chorister, starting with the skin, then intestines, then choral and then went back and did it all over again.

Once it’s all said and done though this is a fantastic sculpt. It's super striking and this guy is Large. In terms of playability, he might be too large. It's gonna be really hard to hide this guy behind most pieces of terrain on your board. That said, it's certainly an imposing silhouette on the battlefield.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!
