title: Trench Crusade Carcass Front Campaign Rules Review
content:
The salt-spewn seas have drawn each of us here. Our patience has paid dividends as we build and paint our warbands in preparation for the call to the front lines. We eagerly gather our friends, bless our sacred dice, and prepare glorious terrain upon which to lay models to rest. It is finally time for us to venture into the Carcass Front!

As a local campaign organizer for my community, I have been so ecstatic since the announcement to see how the creative minds behind Trench Crusade see a narrative campaign unfolding. And I am so happy to say it is just as buck wild and fun as I was hoping. From in-depth and interesting campaign progression, wild and unique missions, and new content to explore and use in all your games; buckle up because the seas are a bit choppy. Let’s swan dive straight into the Carcass Front Campaign!

We would like to thank Factory Fortress Inc for sending us a preview copy of this box for review.

New Patrons

Heretic Captain Credit: Mildnorman

In this campaign we anticipated a faithful and heretical patron aligned with the opposing sides in the region; however the Iron Sultanate tossed their hat in the ring as we have 3 new patrons. The book specifically mentions that all three new Patrons are available not only for Carcass Front, but all campaigns moving forwards. So let's dive headfirst into the deep end with our new leadership.

Blessed Bartolomeo; the Faithful warbands' new patron option. A war prophet that has reached near-sainthood and a vital soul against the heretical efforts on the coast, he offers a multitude of boons that coincide with the theme of pious suffering. With ways to reduce injury rolls, gain blessing markers, and gain flat +Injury Result; Bartolomeo offers all rounded options to warbands looking to survive the cursed war fronts. The Truth of Suffering is a personal stand out choice, offering a flat -1 Dice to injury results targeting the model. The size restraints are minimal, as this model combined with Machine Armour and Martyrdom pills is going to be nearly unkillable.

War Priest Charon; the Heretic warbands' new patron option. We finally get a glimpse at the big bad the Eirie isles has been dealing with, and boy do his visuals sell him well. He offers a surprising amount of movement shenanigans with Wings of Blooded Iron and We are the Storm. Hands down the immediate eye candy though is Master of Death. Automatic 2 to ANY weapon while it is short range with no other limiters is insane. And even if given to a weapon already with automatic, it ups it by 1. Assault Rifles become mobile Machine Guns, Flamethrowers spout even more fire, or double barrel grenade launchers / Anti-Material Rifles wreak mayhem on the field. This ability is going to single handedly push players towards a heretic allegiance.

House of Wisdom; the Iron Sultanate-only new patron option. This was a surprise to see, and a welcome addition to the pool of patrons. If you love the customization that House of Wisdom gives, this patron is going to captivate you wholly. From ignoring keywords, stealing ammo, and mutating our normal lads like they are Tawkin (love me some more mutations); there is so much customization and depth that this Patron offers. The mutation skills are a personal favorite of mine, but the additional keyword ignoring offered by Elemental Savant is going to always be universally good. If it weren’t for Charon, I think House of Wisdom might have stolen the show.

Path to Leviathan

Beyond the map based campaign that is Carcass Front, there is also the narrative campaign Path to Leviathan. This is designed for two opposing warbands, one faithful and one fallen, as they compete for their patrons during the narrative that unfolds. This is not a restriction but a recommendation, as any warbands and their variants can very easily be utilized for this narrative campaign.

The campaign utilizes five scenarios in a set order from the Carcass Front scenario list. They could be played as one-off games with no campaign steps or exploration, or as a campaign following either the Core Rulebook rules or Carcass Fronts version. Regardless of what you choose, the story told will remain the same as two warbands uncover the Path to Leviathan and the treacherous plot at hand.

The Narrative

Sacred Affliction Ecclesiastic Prisoner - bre4d_

In warning to the faithful, the Lord of Hosts sent a vision to Gaius, the Prophet of Mud, of the Procession of the Sacred Affliction. The vision prophesied the expected return of Leviathan, a titanic monster created by the Lord. Gripped with Envy and Desire, the great beast once attempted to take more than their station allowed, and so God trapped the beast in the Abyss, chained and alone. Now those chains begin to break, and so the Lord tasked those of faith to ensure Leviathan never roams the seas or ascends once again. 

The prophecy of Leviathan is no longer something of myth, for Blessed Bartholomeo, a member of the Sacred Affliction, has witnessed the great Serpent itself. They have witnessed the Seven Golden Stars fall, and the Abyss tremor in response. Bartholomeo sees the opportunity to not only defeat the beast, but consume it, and wear its mighty scales as armour, for the glory of God and those of the true faith. 

It is not only the faithful who have become aware of Leviathan’s possible return, for the War Priest Charon aims to ensure the beast’s return and supplant the head of the Serpent of Envy, with their reward in becoming a lord of Hell himself. 

The narrative of the Leviathan campaign unfolds across several scenarios. Players start out searching for the knowledge to summon and bind Leviathan in the Ruins of Nineveh Novus, find the necessary materials to ensure the binding succeeds in the Steel Necropolis, and ultimately decide the fate of Leviathan at their Alter. The important point is that the ending of a campaign depends on the winning side, Faithful or Heretical.

How It Works

As mentioned, the Leviathan campaign can be played as a series of one-off games or as a campaign, increasing your Ducat limit each game, and with all the post-game experiences that come with it. There are 5 scenarios on offer, and players may choose to play those 5, extend the campaign by using regular scenarios from the Core Rule Book, or use the Random Scenario Generator. The only important points are to play the Leviathan Scenarios in order, with the Altar of Leviathan being the last campaign game. 

As with the Carcass Front campaign, players may choose one of the new Patrons released: Blessed Bartholomeo, War-Priest Charon, and the House of Wisdom Patron. You can, of course, pick one of the other Patrons from the Core Rulebook. 

Ultimately, there are 3 possible outcomes in the campaign: a draw, a minor victory for one player, or a major victory for one player. 

  • Draw: This occurs if neither player can summon the great beast
  • Minor Victory: A player manages to summon Leviathan, but is not able to subdue the beast, as they do not control the Railway Cannon from Scenario 4: The Sword of God. 
  • Major Victory: A player manages to summon and subdue the beast, succeeding in achieving their ultimate goal of controlling the beast. 

Carcass Front Campaigns

Lazarist Castigator. Credit: Dandy

Why have we all gathered in the Carcass Front? Some fight for the church after hearing the calls of Bartolomeo requests for aid, while others heed the warchants of Charon. Regardless of how they came to be here, all are here for the same reason; something churns in the ocean deep that can dictate the outcome of the war in this region. Some may be here to stop this effort, spurn it forward, or gather riches while others are distracted thusly.

What makes this campaign unique amongst others? Typically campaigns follow a fairly linear format; players play progressive games and progress accordingly in very similar fashions with the same goals. The Carcass Front campaign pushes this idea beyond that standard however. Due to the implementation of vision cards randomly dictating players goals in the campaign, resources offer multiple ways for scoring Victory Points additionally, and scoring based off the campaign tracker. There are far more ways to score than just the scenarios that take place and battles that occur.

Another important addition is the determination of Aggressor and Battle Zone when playing your games. The Aggressor is the player who has been the Aggressor fewest between the players battling, roll-off for ties, and they will choose the Battle Zone. There are a few rules for determining the battle zone as well; it must be either linked to your entry zone, previously scouted, or linked to a scouted zone.

Each warband’s starting zone on the map is also their war camp! Over time, warbands will have opportunities to grow this camp by adding buildings to them or upgrading previously built buildings. There are four different buildings with three tiers of upgrades for warbands to build: Depot, Garrison, Shrine, and Vault. They can add direct effects such as influencing exploration rolls, gaining resources, or gaining other powerful effects.

Overall, there’s a lot of extra stuff to track here in addition to your standard campaign homework. If you’re a practiced trenchie looking for something new after your fifth campaign, this is a good way to spice things up. If you’re relatively new to the game, maybe hold off on this one unless you wanna dive head first into the deep end.

The Map

The main draw of the campaign is the campaign map. The map adds another dimension to how players can interact with the system. The map is a network of lines from the outer edges that converge on the Altar of Leviathan, with location nodes peppered throughout. Each of these locations are designed to feel special, with none feeling like filler. From the very start of the campaign player choice of direction and exploration matters.

The campaign starts with the determination of Entry Zones which dictates the starting location for players on the map. With four options to choose from, it will be vital for warbands to make this choice carefully, as each has their own pluses and minuses. Each Entry Zone is set on the sides of the map, allowing players to determine what their avenue of entry will be, with each starting zone having two connected zones, none standing above the rest for connectivity. It's worth noting that with only four starting zones, you’ll likely have folks sharing entry zones and that’s fine. This isn’t a “Paint the map” campaign where you’ll be taking control from each other. Instead its more about where you choose to invest and explore to gain resources.

Speaking of resources, each territory you have an outpost in gives you some. Each territory has a series of letters correlating to the Resources; F - Favor, R - Relics, S - Supplies, T - Territories. All four options can score you additional Victory points, but they also offer additional bonuses that make them worth pursuing depending upon your warband's intentions. Glory seekers may prefer favor, whereas those wishing to explore every corner of the map might prefer Territories. Your choices of zone exploration will affect how you interact with the campaign directly.

Vision Cards

Stigmatic Nun. Credit: Dandy

The Vision Deck is a pack of 16 cards which are distributed to each player at the beginning of the campaign. Each player is dealt two cards and they can pick one to commit to for the campaign. The cards themselves are relatively straight forward, asking for objectives like “scout a bunch of territories” or “have a bunch of your guys die.” These cards are dealt in secret and chosen in secret, as they are your warband's true goals guided by your patron. This means that each player will be after differing goals entirely, their actions and choices in the game being altered towards their goals creating unique playthroughs for each participant.

On these cards will be three goals to complete, with the rewards being cumulative for final scoring at the end of the campaign when it is revealed. With only 16 cards in the deck, you’ll run out of cards to deal after eight players. The book recommends adding more vision packs, but you can also take the discarded cards and divvy them out to remaining players. That said, this means players who pick later will have less choice and will be working with cards other players have deemed more difficult to do, so you’ll want to be careful with this.

Campaign Phase

Once you’re all set up you can start playing games. First you’ll select your Battle Zone and your Scenario based on that. After you play your game the steps you’ll take will depend on if you were the Aggressor or not. If you won the game as the Aggressor, you’ll gain two resources from the zone, mark off a win in your tracker, and add the zone you played in to your “Scouted zones” (basically tracking where you’ve played) and add an Outpost to it. If you lost, you only get 1 Resource, but still scout the zone. Regardless you’ll explore, gaining ducats equal to 5x your roll. The non-aggressor meanwhile will always gain a Resource from the zone and gain ducats via an exploration roll (but won’t explore!), but you’ll scout the area and get an outpost if you win.

Note: It’s worth mentioning the book somewhat contradicts itself here. The Post Game Summary block says you’ll always scout as the non-Aggressor and can never build an Outpost, where the rules in those sections reflect the above. This will likely get clarified quickly after release, but for now we recommend going with the rules in the appropriate sections.

This is a pretty major departure from standard campaigns. For one, you’ll only explore in half your games. This is kind of lame, considering exploration is one of the most exciting parts of the post game step, but there are no blank parts of the table in Carcass Front campaigns, so on average you’ll get results just as much and every resource has you explore for free when you get the second resource of a type. Next, you’re only gaining 5x the roll in Ducats, not 10x. You’ll be getting gear and money from Supply related explorations, so if you want to ramp up, that’s the way to do it.

There are two new steps after your games: the Campaign Tracker Step & the Outposts Step. The Campaign Tracker Step has you update the Campaign Tracker (included in the box) based on the results of the game. As these boxes are filled out in the tracker, VP and campaign bonuses will be unlocked and scored over time. These bonuses can be things like rolls on the exploration table, bonus Resources, more Exploration Dice, and exploration skills.

The most impactful bonuses though are the Campaign Buildings you’ll build as you gain as you collect resources. As you gain resources (at 3, 8 and 13 obtained) you’ll unlock a new tier of building. Every first tier gives you the ability to manipulate your exploration rolls on the relevant table by 1; the second tier will always give you an additional dice when rolling on those tables as well as a special bonus, and tier 3 gives you another special bonus. Supplies will build a Depot, which can increase your Threshold Value by a whopping 200 points at tier 2 and the ability to remove a Scar and Trauma from your guys at tier 3. Territories will build a Garrison, which lets you reduce the cost of Glory Items purchased from a merchant by 1 (this is a common result from Territory exploration tables) at tier 2 and give you a free Mercenary at tier 3.  Favour will build the Shrine which gives you a free Advancement for a model with Leader at Tier 2 and Strong and +1 Injury in melee for a model in your warband at tier 3. Lastly, there’s the Vault which is built from relics, which gives you two picks from a list of results on the exploration table instead of 1 at tier 2, and a free Glory item at tier 3.

This means players will likely want to specialize in one or two resources, but dipping into a few gives you a wide range of bonuses. These are also quite thematic which will let you play into the themes of your warband and help fill any gaps. This adds some really neat player expression to the campaign step and gives you some fun milestones to go for.

During the Outpost Step, the winning player will build an outpost in the battle zone that was selected prior to the battle. A warband can only have one outpost per zone, but any number of different warbands can have an outpost in the same zone. These outposts provide a defense bonus of starting units with shovels and cover while battling within their battle zone, a potential scoring bonus at the end of campaign to the player with the most, and there are special zones that grant passive bonuses like half priced armor or weapons if you have an outpost there.

Lastly we have the reworked Exploration Step. The Aggressor will always scout the battle zone post match, but the opposing player will only end up scouting if they won the match. We also have a special Exploration Table to roll on which includes number rangers instead of flat numbers (1-3 vs 2). 

Only the Aggressor will roll on the table however, when the other player rolls their exploration they only get their Ducats from the roll unless they roll 3 matching numbers. If they do, then the agents of Rudolph's Folly (a mercenary air group) will aid them in their next game. This manifests in either a strafing run, which is a multi step attack process where you can shoot a bunch of enemy models, or an aerial bombardment. The bombardment is an odd one as it has you print out a paper circle, hold it in your hand above the battlefield, and then drop it to see where the bomb lands. 

While this is cute and gives the defender something to hope for when rolling their exploration, this is a bit overdone for what it's bringing to the table. There can be a bit of feels bad when showing up to the game knowing your opponent has a free board wide threat and its all a bit fiddly in the actual execution. I’m sure Magic the Gathering old heads are stoked to see the return of Chaos Orb though.

Scenarios

Leviathal Chorus Credit: Mildnorman

First off, those from way back before Trench Crusade 1.0 will remember the original Random Scenario Generator. I am happy to say it has returned in full force and as an even cleaner four page spread. This is immediately getting printed out for one off battle usage at game nights! All our favorite missions and deployments return with some cleanup and polishing.

As far as the actual campaign scenarios, you get five to pick from with one, The Altar of Leviathan, being tied to the endgame of the campaign. The scenarios themselves will be familiar to veterans of the trenches, tasking you with carrying markers, holding key points and doing actions for scoring. The scenarios are symmetrical so you and your opponent will be trying to accomplish the same tasks. 

There’s a double edged aspect to all these scenarios in that they all have bespoke models and terrain. Two have NPC models that will wander the table and attack your guys and the other 3 have terrain pieces that go with them. Smartly, the TC team have included ways to represent them with things you may have lying around and it seems you’ll be able to print most of them either via STL or 2d image on cardboard, but it still feels like just more stuff you’re gonna have to carry to your games. The upside is these make the missions all feel significant and bombastic, like you’re fighting over actual locations with actual personalities instead of “ruined city #5”.

Final Thoughts

Brandon “Zaros” Oelfke: I think there is so much content that for those who have been playing Trench Crusade for a while, this is a treasure trove. I think the true Carcass Front campaign is really complex for new players and definitely the narrative of Path to Leviathan should be the new player focus before throwing them in the deep end of Carcass Front. The new patrons are absolutely wild, and the addition of an Iron Sultanate one was a pleasant surprise. I think this campaign box is going to be an absolute blast for everyone and was definitely worth the wait.

Norman: Echoing Brandon’s point there’s definitely a lot here. I think there’s a ton of smart moves, having the path to leviathan campaign is great for folks looking to get started with this box and and random scenario generator is good for folks who will gravitate towards one offs. I’m not huge on just how much bespoke stuff this campaign asks for, but to their credit they offer alternatives at every turn. The book and background itself are all very cool, with tons of fun lore sections and art to peruse. If I had to pick something to nitpick, its probably the defender exploration/Rudolphs Folly situation; it feels like an overcomplicated solution to a somewhat simple problem. I have no doubt though this will be a blast to go through with friends.

DGMP: This very much feels like something meant for people who already have a campaign or two under their belts and is more complicated to give them more systems to fiddle with and sink their teeth into. And in my opinion it really succeeds with that, adding a lot of new bits and bobs to mess with and see how they work. Plus I have always been a sucker for a good map based campaign. But it is very much not something I would suggest you start out playing. Path to Leviathan is what you should do as a starter, this feels like something you set up for a play group to go through over a month or two to try out a new campaign system. My only real complaints are very small, a few quibbles over exactly how a thing is worded or not having certain information clearly explained or stated where it is located. But overall, I really think this will be a great experience to go through with your local group, if you have at least 4 players. I don’t think it would be at its full potential with less than that.  Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Warhammer 40k's surprising new codex reveal could be a huge lore win, or a power creep disaster
content:
On Monday, Games Workshop revealed huge changes to the rules for Space Marines which will arrive in their new Warhammer 40k codex in October. The Marines will be deadlier and more survivable than ever, and points increases to accompany the buffs. If everything is balanced correctly then Space Marines could be just as much of an elite force on the tabletop as they always have been in Black Library novels. If not, this edition is charging headlong into power creep.

While the Space Marines codex will be the first place these changes are printed, all the variant Space Marine chapters will receive similar upgrades. According to GW spokesperson Eddie Eccles, the codex supplements for Blood Angels, Dark Angels, Space Wolves, and Black Templars will be retired and replaced with a "big digital update", while Grey Knights and Heretic Astartes will get updated datasheets to tide them over until their new 11th edition Warhammer 40k codex releases. Where this leaves the Deathwatch wasn't stated.

GW went into detail on a few of the stat changes in an article on Warhammer Community. Here's what has been revealed so far:

  • Space Marines in Mk 10 Tacticus Armor will have Toughness 5.
  • Space Marines in Phobos Armor will have an eight inch move.
  • Terminators will have Toughness 6.
  • Basic Chainswords and Knives and Fists will become Strength 5.
  • Bolt Rifles will have two fire modes: Focused Fire, with Heavy, A1, S6, AP-1, and D2; and Saturation, with Assault, A2, S5, and D1. Both modes will have Rapid Fire 1, 24" range, and BS3+.
  • Storm Bolters will be Strength 5.

These changes will be accompanied by points increases, which should result in Space Marine armies shrinking slightly. From a lore perspective that's a huge win. Space Marines are supposed to be elite troops powerful enough to conquer the entire galaxy, but on the tabletop they have typically been right in the middle of the factions.

From a gameplay balance perspective this is going to be a challenge for the designers. You can analyse the points efficiency of a unit's damage output and survivability fairly easily, but it's far harder to quantify the impact of an army's board presence and maneuverability, which is the key to actually winning scenarios.

Given that Space Marines of various flavors make up about half of the total Warhammer 40k factions, the designers also have a lot of plates to spin. Removing two units from a 2,000 point army has a very different impact on the fast-moving Space Wolves compared to the trudging Death Guard. Most Marine armies have big model ranges and may be able to lean on non-infantry units that (presumably) won't be affected, but the Emperor's Children and Grey Knights will be particularly exposed thanks to their limited ranges and focus on infantry.

Then there's the risk of power inflation. Many units have their current power level fixed relative to that of the Space Marines - Necrons have always been roughly equivalent, Custodes slightly more powerful, bolt weapons used by other armies have been on par with their Space Marine equivalents, and so on. Is GW going to increase their power and points costs accordingly?

An even power increase across many armies would just result in the game needing fewer models to play. That would be welcome on the wallet and make games quicker, but wouldn't really make the Marines feel more elite. If GW doesn't maintain the relative strengths and weaknesses that have existed between factions in the past, can it create a new equilibrium?

It's all speculation until we get our hands on the new codex, of course. What do you think is mostly likely? I'd love to hear your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Magic: The Gathering Mystery Booster: Commander Edition Review, Part 1 of 2 – Multicolor Cards
content:
Magic’s depths know no end, and Mystery Booster: Commander Edition is nothing but the deepest of cuts. Whether torn from the annals of history, video games older than multiple Tabletop Battles site authors, or offhand flavor text, this set is one for Magic’s most entrenched players. It introduces new ways to bend the rules of Commander, via the Rulebreaker mechanic, but even those cards without that exact line still do so in spirit; this is a weird set, and we’re all thrilled to dive into it. This week, we’re covering the set’s Multicolored & Colorless options, from a Commander which lets you play a 10,000 card deck, to Magic’s first true non-permanent Commander.

Mystery Booster: Commander Edition officially releases on November 9th via Festival in a Box, but is exclusively available until then at official Magiccons & Commandfests. Actually acquiring these cards isn’t likely to be easy, especially until November, but in theory you could play against them right now at your LGS, hence our coverage.

Multicolor

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Venser, Visionary Traveler

Saffgor: I’ve already covered Venser in a Puzzlebox, but I think he’s more of an aristocrats Commander than a blink one. Obvious loops with Persist, Guardian of the Forgotten, and some cool tech like Reweaveing into Ugin, Eye of the Storms has the makings of a very nifty deck. Folks have written him off as a worse blink Commander than existing options, and they’re right to do so, but peer beyond the veil and you’ve got something wildly unique. The hidden gem of the Multicolor cards here.

BPhillipYork: Given how many things key off power or toughness, or use counters to do random stuff, the built in "passive" ability here is pretty easy to abuse with various creatures. Combined with the the ability to flicker creatures effectively lets you set up combos. The obvious one is Sage of Hours and The Ozolith and resourceful defense. Flickering creatures to move counters onto the sage will let you take infinite turns pretty easily. But there's plenty of other ways to get enormous value out of flickering things.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Whtz, the Bibliophile

Saffgor: A cool card in theory, that’s for sure. In practice, however, a Whtz deck loses focus fast, and descends into becoming a goodstuff 250+ card pile, an Azorius slurry buoyed by having access to Yorion as a companion. For all the people excited to build this and Battle of Wits, I ask…why? The payoff is winning the game with a meandering upkeep trigger, on an expensive card telegraphed by virtue of your deck being stored in a shoebox. Whtz isn’t clever, it isn’t nuanced. It’s goodstuff with a win condition that rewards you for playing goodstuff, in sufficient quantity, and annoys your opponents when you’re forced to shuffle.

BPhillipYork: This is already spawning huge decks, a 200 card deck isn't so bad, and conceivably of course you could just run 100 persistent petitioners and automill people out. The practicalities of a 200 card deck though kind of make me frustrated. It's almost performative, especially if the person has to shuffle a lot, it's just going to be a painful Mr. Bean sort of sketch where you sit and watch the person. And I don't like decks that create that environment, which is basically, hey, watch me jerk off. It's almost implicitly a rule 0 violation, which fundamentally should start with 'let everyone have fun.'

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

The Weaver King

Saffgor: A bit on the slow side, but it’s cool to see an Afterlife from the Loam as a combat damage trigger. Seems like a blast in Bracket 2, so long as everyone’s battlecruiser-ing it up.

BPhillipYork: Well, slamming into people, force milling them, and then getting those creatures isn't particularly strong given it costs 6 mana. However it's pretty consistent, and if you run a bunch of other mill and then get that to trigger off first so you get to look through a lot of cards to see what you want, it's fairly powerful. If you combine it with some early game stax and control it's probably a pretty powerful deck vs creature heavy archetypes.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Sifa Grent

Saffgor: Blood Artist as a static ability, and the capacity to make your opponents fight? Smells like a fun casual politics Commander, and as an added bonus, quite enjoys Crime triggers. Like all Planeswalker Commanders with access to Red, she can be Reality Scrambled into a different walker of your choice, so be aware of that as an option, when thinking on practical win conditions.

BPhillipYork: This is the kind of planeswalker that has a powerful ability that seems like it's just going to get her killed unless you have a really good way of protecting her.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Ashaya’s Enduring Bond

Saffgor: The first non-permanent Commander, cool! I definitely want to cover the Bond in greater detail, but I’d position this card as a Bard Class ‘Secret Commander’, with a ton of {R}{G}-cost Legends that are free under the class, and enable you to cast this Legendary Sorcery. I don’t think this is a powerful Commander, but it absolutely gets the gears turning.

BPhillipYork: I like the random aspect of running some kind of mana power up deck that just casts this over and over. I really quite like this mechanic where paying more commander tax actually nets you something. I'm sad that WotC doesn't seem to return to it often, but building around a sorcery is totally a fun new deckbuilding challenge.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Grizzlegom, Hurloon Hero

Saffgor: For all of the color identity rulebreakers, you need to ask yourself “Would I play this if it were just printed as 5C?”, because in essence that’s what they allow, to a lesser extent. For Grizzlegom, I think the answer is a strong maybe, because for what he lacks in the capacity to come down early, he makes up for in one huge swing. There’s a few ways to make your Lands all basic types, and if you scrape away the text from this card and just let those abilities count Lands, period, attacking with Grizzlegom is akin to casting an Ultimatum. Weird card, fairly obvious, but a Timmy slam dunk.

BPhillipYork: This is okay, but it just sort of reeks of running an insanely expensive mana base if you don't proxy cards, and then just running every dual-typed land you can and then running maybe an ETB deck. Funny that the mountain and swamp abilities are basically the worst of them.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Elda, Conjuror of Spectacle

Saffgor: Bet you didn’t expect her to be seeing cEDH experimentation. Yes, Elda is in discussions as a tournament cEDH option, for her capacity to force draws with Charismatic Conqueror, and spread hatebears across the board like Collector Ouphe. Getting rid of one Drannith Magistrate is easy, but what about three? She gets markedly worse if draws stop counting for points in tournament play, but as it stands she’s essentially taken the spot of GW Selvala as the ‘wait, she does what?’ Selesnya Commander of the format.

BPhillipYork: I'm sure there's some kind of fun and sort of fair way to play this card, though to me it seems like it'll get abused by people basically just handing their friend the win, which I really don't like. There is a lot of synergy with group hug type creature cards and then you'll be drawing a lot. If all your opponents are drawing extra cards which causes you to draw extra cards, and your deck is like, 40% ramp by volume then you're probably the only one who can really take advantage of it. But this feels like it might lead to a lot of unfun games.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Selenia, the Cursed Heart

Saffgor: Very unhinged rattlesnake effect on this card, sheesh. Don’t make the Selenia player angry, or you’ll be booted from the game at Mach 5; I do think she’s a bit costly to be a real threat, but the political chit of doling out a Curse as strong as hers is very compelling.

BPhillipYork: I think the lifegain is pretty gross potentially, there's a couple of these doublers, actually 6 total, so you can get insane life totals, but then what do you do with that. Aside from just lasering people with Aetherflux Reservoir there's not a ton of things, still having this ability in the Command Zone is potentially pretty good, and then having a threat from killing your commander is an interesting effect.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Itazura, Lingering Wick

Saffgor: Room 8 Studio, the folks behind this card’s art, has a history of implementing GenAI in their workflow. Make of that what you will. Itazura is weird and gimmicky, but this is much like the one ghastly Gruul Toph in being a card I just can’t support. There’s been no statement, but if it quacks like a duck…

BPhillipYork: I hate this. It turns every upkeep into a guessing game while people figure out the "meta" of what damage to take, but then there's every incentive to fill your deck with garbage. Wheel of Misfortune takes long enough to resolve, I'd hate having to do it every turn.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Davvol, Evincar of Rath

Saffgor: This isn’t exactly Carnival of Souls, as it only checks your board, but this is plenty neat regardless. There’s a fair few combos available to Davvol, but even from a fair angle he’s akin to a Black Birgi in the Command Zone, and that’s sure to enable some fun pop-off turns. Happy birthday buddy!

BPhillipYork: So this is obviously kind of a combo card. Black and Green gives you access to a fair amount of life gain to overcome this, and just sets you up to go off from the Command Zone with a massive enabler. Right off the bat with something like a Gravecrawler, a sac outlet, and a couple of lifegain triggers you go infinite, so you know, basic black building blocks, but that's largely all the deck can do.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Chief Magistrate of Mercadia

Saffgor: An incredibly cool card to see from a story perspective, but sadly not a strong one. You really want to be flashing this in to ensure the best version of its upkeep trigger, and that’s not the easiest in Boros.

BPhillipYork: Given that just copying creatures as tokens has become so prevalent this has the potentially to be a game winner, but you have to stay the monarch and he doesn't exactly enable that scenario. Feels like a commander that wins off of a Final Fortune, but that has a very laying it all out there feel.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Rikala, Homarid King

Saffgor: Another banger, good lord. Played fairly, Rikala gives you a modest board buff for your attackers, and a turn of High Tide, all thematically great and very much in like with the OG Homarid. Why bother playing fair though? Rikala is a premier Commander for non-combo counter shenanigans, providing potential for huge damage via your evasive creatures, wearing doubled counters well, and even rewarding you for playing a sufficient density of Stifles. No matter how unfair Rikala gets though, even if he’s providing a board +8/+0 and doubling your mana, he’s still…weirdly fair, in the grand scheme of things. Winner of a card, especially for those Simic-curious.

BPhillipYork: Fun to see a call back all the way to Forgotten Empires, which is sadly largely forgotten except the odd Thrull or Saproling creature. This is basically just Tidal Influence, the card, though definitely stronger. It would be pretty neat to see a bunch of Homarids get printed, especially if they all care about how many tide counters your permanents have.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Lyna, Veil of Vengeance

Saffgor: There are shades of Breena, the Demagogue at play here, helping Creatures from various players get in (or not be able to block). Lyna’s power really hinges on how combat-centric a given set of decks are, though, because on its own she’s paying quite the premium to dole out unblockable and draw a few cards. Perhaps she’s best in a stax shell, to make combat matter more? There’s something here, but in passive pods I doubt she gets enough value.

BPhillipYork: Yeah this is a way to make a basically non-interactive deck. Shadow creatures are fine, with access to all of Esper you get about 20 playable ones, slam into your opponents, drawing cards and dealing damage and then anthem-ing for a win. Another option of course is to use this to make creatures that you really don't want to connect just go right through with shadow. With the slow drip of shadow stuff there should be some way to punish shadow or protect yourself from it, and I'm not talking Circle of Protection: Shadow or Aether Web.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

The Madcap Jester

Saffgor: People have talked about this in a cEDH context, but the fact he himself only exiles on attack might make this jester a bit too funny to actually hit those heights. Still, the fact you can yoink combo pieces from an opponent via Bitter Ordeal and dedicate no room in your own deck to wincons is an upside! The bigger problem is that a Jester played in a pod without combos is going to feel middling at best, and as such this is likely to be a card with a skewed reputation.

BPhillipYork: Sort of a fun way to just have lots of ramp and interaction and then play off your opponents' decks.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Tresserhorn’s Lord, Returned

Saffgor: The Lord is very much like an inverted Beza, the Bounding Spring, asking you to fulfill three very Grixis conditions and play from ahead, as opposed to behind. More important, though, is the fact that you can finally get your friends to consider not playing Korvold. Look, drawing cards when sacrificing is fun and powerful, but Korvold homogenized the entire archetype under his devious talon. The Lord is probably the closest thing we’ve seen to a true competitor.

BPhillipYork: Fun call back to Legends, pretty playable and actually can get pretty gross if you set up the right conditions, though sort of just a Grixis version of the existing Jund Korvold, Fae-Cursed King which is already kind of an all-star commander.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

The Muckslinger Gang

Saffgor: This level of weirdness is exactly what I want to see from a set like this; at first the utility of the Gang’s abilities seems low, but between Flings, surviving damage-based wipes, fight spells, crewing/stationing, etc there’s a whole host of benefits to being +3/+3 bigger outside of combat. This is a brewer’s dream, although part of me worries it would lead to decks that ended up too Commander-reliant.

BPhillipYork: +3/+3 is nice but not so big really. Fun for like fighting type things and biting or whatever. Also, yeah you could do Fling type effects, but so what, and if your deck is built around that they'll just kill your commander I would assume. Probably the biggest is just surviving -X/-X board clears repeatedly, but as soon as you use one of those sorcery speed spells I think your commander will just bite it unless you've set up hexproof already.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Jandor, Fortuned Traveler

Saffgor: Wolf as a type to mount is a bit weird, but Jandor’s a great little buildaround for all the Mount-matters cards from Thunder Junction & Aetherdrift. For a pod that doesn’t intend to combo, dedicating an extra body to drawing a card, buffing an attacker, and making a Food is a pretty sweet deal, but don’t skimp on existing Mount options either!

BPhillipYork: This is fun, probably not good, throw in small creatures, any creatures that do helpful things when they tap (Magda, Brazen Outlaw is a perfect example and then just, whale away. If you can turn your foods into creatures that would be really funny, if not good. Sadly most of the really abusive things you can do with food are in black, so out of color identity, but there's plenty of "when you gain life" triggers in green and white, so probably just use them that way.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Feroz, Ulgrotha’s Warden

Saffgor: The most interesting thing Feroz does is create his signature Ban, and that’s not a terribly fun card to sit across from. Bant can then duplicate the token, protect the Bans, etc, but Feroz himself is too expensive and likely too slow to make it in B4. He’s a design without a home, in my eyes, and that’s a real shame.

BPhillipYork: There's enough planeswalker commander now that you could certainly have planeswalkers commander games, which maybe is the point, though the meta shifts dramatically if you do that. Suddenly you don't have to worry about your commander being trivially taken out easily, and lots of people may run mass board clears from damage, via spells like Earthquake that will leave the planeswalkers alone. This is a sort of weird, Bant goodstuff commander, though the idea of stacking up Feroz's Bans and shutting down creature decks is kind of amusing, especially with blue to return to hand.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Olag and Miau, New Friends

Saffgor: This is more a changeling deck than it is one for Zombies or Cats, but funny enough due to Amonkhet we have a weirdly high number of existing Zombie Cats (8, including this card). Still, that Throne of the God-Pharaoh effect for your relevant types will stack up in terms of damage pretty quickly, so I could see this working.

BPhillipYork: I don't know, cats and zombies, I guess that's thing, or maybe I am just not following closely enough. I guess you'd just run a bunch of cats and zombies, pretty straightforward.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Massimo, the Magician

Saffgor: Never was there ever a cat so clever as magical Mr. Massimo here. Between his capacity to combo off with The Great Train Heist, duplicate tutors and dig for combo pieces in one go, and come down shockingly early alongside his cheap, evasive peers, Massimo is a premier tempo Commander across pretty much all power levels. You don’t even need to worry about permanently losing options either, with Pull From Eternity!

BPhillipYork: This is fun but pretty good, and will probably get out of control and turn your deck into archenemy all the time. Like, you just run a bunch of utility spells and evasion creatures, loot or rummage into your yard, and then you're casting tons of spells each turn. It's a fun deck concept, but has so much snowball potential that it seems like Massimo will frequently eat a Path to Exile or something as soon as the cat wizard enters.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Homer, the Hermit

Saffgor: Jury’s out on this one until we get Nauctis: The Sunken Realm next year, wherein we’ll probably see the number of cards with the types mentioned double. The payoff itself is solid, and really more of a self-mill tool until you’ve found an infinite Landfall engine with which to mill your opponents out.

BPhillipYork: That's potentially a grotesque amount of mill popping off, Sultai can land ramp very effectively and do graveyard recursion. Your Crabs, Lobsters, Nautiluses, Starfish and Trilobites can be a bit pricey, though to me the obvious solution is just to use things that can clone Homer and not die, which there are a fair amount of now, and suddenly you're getting multiple landfall triggers of twice X multiple times per turn. Gross.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Uugguu, the Omniplasm

Saffgor: Less interesting than Ratadrabrik of Urborg or Princess Yue as a cloning pile, but likely more resilient. The fact that your first clone ends up with 3 copies of Uugguu is solid, and if you get board wiped, those copies see the original and turn into 4 Uugguu post-wipe. The bigger issue is that Oozes aren’t wildly out of line in terms of power, when we’re looking at cards to copy, so beyond being a resilient clone strategy you’d need to weave in Arcane Adaptation-style effects to get appropriate value at high B3/4. Not a huge fan, but there’s potential.

BPhillipYork: Oozes be oozing and more or less reproducing through fragmentation. Since it's Sultai you can be sacrificing and recurring, making hordes of Ooze, if that's your thing. It just all feels a bit obvious.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Tsagan, Raider Warlord

Saffgor: This is a first—an Alchemy card ported into paper, legal for Commander. We’ve had this before, but never with a real stamp, and it sets an exciting precedent. As for Tsagan himself, this is probably the best Speed Commander available, and represents a ton of aggro pressure in an archetype all about aggressive play. I covered Speed in the context of Commander in a Puzzlebox, but the biggest recommendation I have for Tsagan is to play for the pregame actions, and mulligan aggressively. There are many worlds where he comes down and you’re already at Max Speed, or minimum 3.

BPhillipYork: So at max speed your creatures get +1/0 for each creature your control, which is a fairly hefty bump in power, also handing out first strike to a bunch of creatures makes it them difficult to block. To me though this sort of screams unblockable creatures that just slam into your opponents, so like shadow, which tend to be small and cheap, but if each of them is getting +S, then you need something like 7-8 creatures to kill all your opponents in one turn with 2 power shadow creatures. That's not hard to accomplish at all. Of course you can also just make a go-wide token creature deck and then you'll have no trouble hitting that also.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Zagorka, Mother of Sanctum

Saffgor: I’m not a group hug player, so I can’t really get in the correct headspace to evaluate this card. Zagorka looks…bad, to such an extent she’s probably worse than generic Temur options like Partners for the colors. I guess the idea is that you provide opponents Lands, and they fight amongst themselves?

BPhillipYork: I don't know about this. It seems like when they want to attack you they just won't take the tokens. IMO these lands should create a basic War Tax, where the lands have a built in "that player must be pay X for each Sanctum you control to attack the player whose ability created these tokens". That's a mouthful of an ability, but to me this is like, okay right I'm going to take the Sanctums until I'm ready to kill you.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Arzakon

Saffgor: Arzakon exists for one reason only: Cloning Black Lotus. Token copies, animation + Populate, you name it. You can create a board worth more than many houses, if we take the real card’s value as that of the tokens. Is he worse than Garth One-Eye? Perhaps, but given he can come down and create the token without need of haste, that could be the difference maker.

BPhillipYork: I guess, why not just give him the other abilities too. Give him Giant Growth and Healing Salve. This obsession with Black Lotus tokens is dumb to me.

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Nephilim Epochal

Saffgor: This is a band-aid on the wound that has existed in Commander since the format's inception: The original 4-color Nephilim aren't Legendary. I don't think this card is especially good, but what it does accomplish is in allowing you to play any (or all) as 'secret Commanders'. It isn't great, but the Epochal does soothe the soul of the format.

BPhillipYork: Well now you can make your legal Nephilim deck. There aren't actually enough Nephilim for this to be anything other than a stunt, but now they will probably make more.

Colorless

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

The Everforger

Saffgor: I think this is honestly way cooler in the 99 than the Command Zone, so it being Colorless is a huge boon! This is a nifty secondary option for Myr typal, which is where my head goes to immediately, but I could also see it playing well with all the Job Select Equipment from Final Fantasy. Neat card, and I'll see about jamming it in Sanwell, Avenger Ace's 99.

BPhillipYork: This is pretty nice, though why it didn't just allow all colored artifacts is beyond me, it's not like that would be so good.

That wraps up our look at the Multicolor and colorless cards of Mystery Booster: Commander Edition. We’ll be back later this week to round them out with Monocolor.

title: MTG Masters of the Universe Secret Lair drop value breakdown
content:
Wizards of the Coast has just announced the Masters of the Universe Secret Lairs it teased at MagicCon, presenting five premium MTG card collections themed around He-Man and pals.

There's some fantastic artwork in this drop, and a lot of care was clearly taken to delight fans of the franchise. For everyone else, though, you're probably more interested in the actual reprint value of the cards on show.

Remember that the target here is $29.99 for regular versions or $39.99 for foils, as that's what these will cost from the Secret Lair website. Let's take a look.

 

5. Allies And Enemies Of Eternia

  • Sakashima the Impostor - $15 Nonfoil / $50 Foil
  • Kona, Rescue Beastie - $1.05 Nonfoil / $1.75 Foil
  • Ertai Resurrected - $0.30 Nonfoil / $0.50 Foil
  • Derevi, Empyrial Tactician - $8 Nonfoil / $5.80 Foil
  • Samut, Voice of Dissent - $2.20 Nonfoil / $5.75 Foil
  • Tetsuo, Imperial Champion - $0.55 Nonfoil / $0.95 Foil
  • Total = $27.10 Nonfoil / $64.75 Foil

Starting off with a bunch of side characters, and while I commend Wizards on its reskin choices (which I think actually fit pretty well for once) there's not a lot of value outside of Sakashima.

Luckily, Sakashima is a $15/$50 card, really rescuing this Lair. If you don't want the blue card, you should probably skip this one unless you particularly like the characters.

4. Sold Separately

  • Fortune, Loyal Steed - $0.30 Nonfoil / $0.40 Foil
  • The Gitrog, Ravenous Ride - $4.45 Nonfoil / $7.10 Foil
  • Throne of the God-Pharaoh - $7.30 Nonfoil / $12 Foil
  • Sword of War and Peace - $11 Nonfoil / $15 Foil
  • Command Tower (Double Sided) - $0.30 Nonfoil / $0.35 Foil
  • Total = $23.35 Nonfoil / $34.85 Foil

In Sold Separately, we have a couple of underwhelming Thunder Junction mounts (which make for less convincing reskins - Panthor doesn't look like a frog horror to me) and some decent artifact cards. But the full art Command Tower is a major unknown and worth giving some thought.

It's an iconic EDH card, but unlike Sol Ring, it doesn't exactly draw attention when it hits the table, perhaps making a flashy one less exciting. Secret Lair Command Towers really vary in price on the secondary market, but having a full art treatment definitely helps. This particular card also has a fun gimmick. It's double-sided, with Castle Grayskull on one side and Snake Mountain on the other, so you can pick your allegiance.

On balance, I expect this card to be pretty sought-after, which is why I'm elevating this Lair to fourth place instead of fifth.

3. By The Power Of Grayskull!

  • Winota, Joiner of Forces - $2.40 Nonfoil / $7.90 Foil
  • Crackle with Power - $7.55 Nonfoil / $11 Foil
  • Delina, Wild Mage - $5.65 Nonfoil / $7.50 Foil
  • Bruenor Battlehammer - $0.65 Nonfoil / $2.20 Foil
  • Konda's Banner - $11.75 Nonfoil / $61 Foil
  • Total = $28 Nonfoil / $89.60 Foil

He-Man helms a very Boros Secret Lair, and I guess the idea here is that you might throw all of these into the same deck… though the synergy isn't exactly obvious.

The most notable card here is Konda's Banner, only ever printed in Champions of Kamigawa back in 2004. That's helped its price tag, despite this being a fairly middling board-buffer, only really useful in a few mono-color tribal decks.

While they made it part of the joke, it's actually quite annoying that you have to pick up He-Man's sword and cat 'separately'.

2. She-Ra, Princess Of Power

  • Sisay, Weatherlight Captain - $2.80 Nonfoil / $7.10 Foil
  • Silence - $7.80 Nonfoil / $8.20 Foil
  • Emiel the Blessed - $14 Nonfoil / $30 Foil
  • Hajar, Loyal Bodyguard - $0.80 Nonfoil / $0.80 Foil
  • Kutzil, Malamet Exemplar - $2.60 Nonfoil / $3.15 Foil
  • Sol Ring - $1.70 Nonfoil / $1.85 Foil
  • Total = $29.70 Nonfoil / $51.10 Foil

The value isn't exactly going up in leaps and bounds, but this is technically worth more than the last Lair. I guess market research must show a lot of overlap between cEDH players and She-Ra lovers, because these are all cards that fans can and do play in competitive Sisay, Weatherlight Captain builds.

This lair is a lot better than the numbers suggest because of that textless, full-art Sol Ring - one of the most talked about cards in this entire superdrop. A good Sol Ring treatment can easily be worth $20-50, and this is the first textless version.

1. Nyah-Ha-Ha!

  • Tinybones, the Pickpocket - $6.05 Nonfoil / $6.50 Foil
  • Tasha's Hideous Laughter - $3.60 Nonfoil / $4.75 Foil
  • Bottomless Pit - $6.20 Nonfoil / $20.60 Foil
  • Necrogen Mists - $11 Nonfoil / $31 Foil
  • Breach the Multiverse - $11 Nonfoil / $11 Foil
    Total = $37.85 Nonfoil / $73.85 Foil

The Skeletor Secret Lair was surely always going to be the most popular - he's the star of all the memes! Wizards has given the villain the best  drop too, with some suitably fiendish discard cards that all work in a Tinybones deck (except the blue one). The value is pretty spread out here, with most of these cards worth more than $5.

I'm keenest on the cheapest card of the lot though - give me that Skeletor's Villainous Glee!

Funnily enough two of these cards have already appeared on another skeleton-themed Secret Lair, Bad to the Bones. In fact, that's the only place you'll find a foil Bottomless Pit.

That's yer lot, and it feels like there's quite a flat curve this time around. There's nothing outrageous for me to get up in arms about - no dreary drop packed with penny cards. On the other hand, the number one Lair isn't an absolute steal either.

The 'The Most Powerful Superdrop In The Multiverse' Secret Lair will release on September 14, and the pre-queue opens at 8am PT. Unlike the recent Hatsune Miku deck, this one's not print-to-demand!

title: GW massacres firstborn Space Marines, sends 17 Warhammer 40k units to Legends
content:
On Monday, Games Workshop took a knife to the Space Marines range, and then plunged it into the hearts of old school players still playing with armies they built during earlier editions of Warhammer 40,000. An article published on Warhammer Community revealed that 12 units will be completely axed from the next Codex: Space Marines, and a further five models will be demoted to serve as proxies for other unit entries. Almost all of the casualties are the older, smaller, 'firstborn' Space Marine models.

Specifically, the following 12 kits will have their rules moved from the Space Marines codex to the Legends supplement. Legends don't receive balance updates and aren't eligible to use in most organised play games, and we can expect these models to leave production:

  • Centurion Assault Squad
  • Centurion Devastator Squad
  • Razorback
  • Predator Destructor
  • Predator Annihilator
  • Vindicator
  • Whirlwind
  • Dreadnought
  • Stormhawk Interceptor
  • Stormtalon Gunship
  • Stormraven Gunship
  • Hammerfall Bunker

The following five units will also not be part of the Space Marines codex, but have instead been redesignated as 'Legendary Proxies'. Their models can be used to stand in for a different unit:

  • Tactical Squad - counts as an Intercessor Squad
  • Devastator Squad - counts as a Desolation Squad
  • Suppressor Squad - counts as an Inceptor Squad
  • Pedro Kantor - counts as a Captain
  • Uriel Ventris - counts as a Captain

This doesn't quite mark the end of the firstborn kits. The Mars pattern Rhino will still be in service, though I have to wonder if its transport capacity will be downgraded to reflect how teeny tiny it looks next to Primaris marines. Several Space Marine chapters still have unique firstborn units, including the Space Wolves Wulfen and Thunderwolf Cavalry, the Deathwatch Watch Master, and almost the entirety of the Grey Knights range.

It's been almost a decade since the first Primaris models were released, and it was only a matter of time before the firstborn Space Marines went the way of the Thunder Warriors. I raise my glass to some very long serving kits, to everyone who just had their armylist gutted, and to YouTuber 'Paul is bad at stuff', who can no longer bring his cursed 36 Centurion list to tournaments.

Bitter as this pill will be to swallow for some 40k players, Heresy players can be cheerier. The price of Predators, Vindicators, and Whirlwinds on eBay and trading groups is likely to crash. The 40k models may not be the Deimos pattern vehicles that are most associated with the Heresy, but the Mars pattern vehicles were just as prevalent on both sides of the conflict.

The fact that the Stormraven is going off sale is also interesting. This ugly flying brick is the base chassis on which the far cooler Storm Eagle and Fire Raptor are built using resin components. If it's being removed from production, there's a chance that GW is making new, completely plastic models for these iconic Heresy aircraft. Given how hellish the current hybrid kits are to build, it's a change I would welcome.

Has your army just been gutted, or are you ready to swoop in and grab some bargains? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: I think I've found my new favorite low-effort pub board game
content:
Let's be honest; if you enjoy 1. drinking alcohol in a pub or bar; 2. playing board games; and 3. doing both of those things at the same time; your options for doing so have become vastly better in recent years. Even if your town is one of the few on earth that hasn't yet sprouted a board game bar, these days you can rock up to a normie watering hole with a couple of games and settle in for a six hour session without even getting funny looks.

Consequently, in the same period we've been blessed with a panoply of new, rules light, short play, small box games that are short on depth, complexity, and moving parts, but long on convenience, speed, and merriment. Legendary pocket rockets Scout and Skull are in our all-time list of the best board games with good reason, and I'll defend them unto death.

But, after snapping up a review copy of the slimmed down, retuned Las Vegas from Ravensburger at Gen Con 2026, I think this might just unseat Scout from my pub night survival kit - for a while at least. That's not because it's 'better', either for my personal tastes or in any objective sense.

Las Vegas, only slightly amended from its original 2016 formula, doesn't deliver anything anywhere near as clever or innovative as Scout's deliciously brain-tickling, double-layered tactical wrangle. To state the obvious, it's not as portable either; tabletop games don't get much more convenient than a hardy little orange box the size of a bar of soap.

No, Las Vegas is coming with me to the pub because its virtues - limited though they may turn out to be in terms of replay appeal - are almost perfectly aligned with my criteria for a game played in one's cups. In my view, a good bar board game needs to:

  • Be very quick and easy to set up, re-rack, and pack away.
  • Have both a short overall play time, and very quick turns, to keep up momentum.
  • Be pretty to look at, but have zero design elements or in-game information you can't learn from a single, rapid, possibly blurry glance in poor lighting.
  • Have simply designed, hardwearing components that can withstand spills and knocks.
  • Have an extremely limited decision space - both to keep things moving, and to stay entertaining amid conversation, noise, distractions, and, er, declining cognitive ability.
  • AND MOST IMPORTANTLY: contain just enough potential for tactical decision making that you always feel invested and impactful - but not so much that you ever have to think very hard about anything.

To be clear, loads of games that don't meet those criteria can be great fun played at the bar while imbibing. Some of the best gaming times I've ever had while drinking were incredibly long, slow, silly games of Scrabble. And of course there's nothing quite like a few hands of Poker when everyone's capacity to remember probabilities or read facial expressions is dropping by 20% every half hour.

But when it comes to what I'd call proper, board game board games - modern, boxed releases that came out this side of the fall of the Berlin Wall - the above formula is what I've found works best for me. And honestly, Las Vegas fits the bill handsomely.

If you never played the 2016 original, I'll skip straight to summarizing the new 2026 version - partly because I never played the original, but mostly because the new one is incredibly similar and, from what I can tell, a better match for my criteria than its predecessor. Don't worry, this won't take long.

There are six cardboard mats on the table, each with a designated number from one to six, themed after non-specific Vegas casinos. Two prize banknotes are laid next to each casino, with values from $10,000 to $100,000.

Each player gets their own colored set of six small D6 dice, and one bigger D6, adorably called the 'biggie' die. Each turn, you roll all the dice you have, then choose one group of matching rolls (all the ones, all the fours, etc.) and place them on the casino matching that number.

Once everyone's rolled and placed all their dice, whoever has most dice on each casino wins the larger of its two cash prizes, and second place gets the smaller one. Your 'biggie', of course, counts for two dice. If any number of players are tied, they all lose, and whoever has the most dice after them wins the big money. After three rounds (or however many you want, honestly), the person with the most cash wins.

Immediately, you've got an unapologetically high-randomness formula here. Any strategy you adopt has to contend not only with your dice rolls, but all your opponents' rolls too. More often than not (especially at higher player counts) someone else will get a bum roll where their choice is to achieve nothing at all, or blow their dice on forcing  a tie, just to rob you of a win. Schadenfreude is ever present.

Thing is, it's also got those magical balancing ingredients of momentum and simplicity. High randomness frequently creates situations that screw over some players and reward others - but you never feel truly shafted, because you never had to invest much brainpower to begin with. And in any case, by the time you've started feeling salty, the Aleae have already been iactae again, and someone else is in the firing line.

For me, the dinky, untaxing little decisions you get to make here are exactly the right level of brainwork for a pub session after work. It's mostly just whether to spend a multi-dice combo in one go, hoping to secure a larger payday, or drop them piecemeal into several casinos, reserving more dice to re-roll and increasing your chances of snagging multiple second prize wins.

Beyond that, it's mostly just chance and banter. If your plan works out, great! If it works out because the late game dice fell just so, nudging your rival out of a big hundred-bag win, even though they dropped five dice there and you just one, even great-er!

If not - if, this time, you were the one nudged out of a payout by lady luck or your mother in law's vindictive whim, for example - well, not to worry. The next round will almost certainly be different, and in any case the banknotes have humourous dice-faced cartoon characters on them, not US presidents. Fundamentally, it's a pretty dumb game - but it's just the right kind of dumb to go perfectly with intoxicating beverages. Plus, rolling dice is always fun forever (even if your father-in-law loses one on the floor every freaking time). Can recommend.

A disclaimer here before I go: as with anything Wargamer publishes on the intersection between tabletop gaming and drinking liquor, we're honor bound to acknowledge that combo isn't for everyone. Not every board gamer likes to drink, and even those that do often prefer to keep the two pleasures separate. Gods know, if your thing is noggin-tangling Euros or six-hour Twilight Imperium marathons, imbibing brain-altering chemicals is unlikely to fit neatly with your hobby experience (although if it does, you know, you do you!)

But for me, just as there's a joy in intrepidly seeking (and then staying within) my body's alcohol limits, there's a parallel pleasure in finding the board games that are precisely the right counterpart to the cognitive level I'm at once optimum buzz has been achieved. Rare is the game that's just as fun for me - or even more so - after three pints of room temperature British ale as it was beforehand. While Las Vegas continues acing that very specific assignment, I shall salute it.

I'm always on the hunt for something even easier, stupider, and just as fun, to play while I dull my existential dread, though - so if you have a better pub game, come join the free Wargamer Discord community and let me know! Alcohol isn't served there, but good vibes run free.

title: D&D's new playtest underwhelms in the Underdark
content:
Put these D&D Underdark subclasses back in their cave, they're clearly not done yet. In the newest playtest document, released August 20, 2026, we received new character options for three classic D&D classes. There's a House Agent Rogue, working for the drow houses; a Path of Unlight Barbarian, surging with unnatural light; and a Imaskarcanist Wizard who can control this same magic glowiness.

There's some nice flavor here, and all three could be interesting to play in a campaign that takes place in the Underdark, even if the word 'unlight' is kinda confusing. But the vibes could be immaculate, it wouldn't change the fact that these subclasses are, from a mechanical standpoint, incredibly weak.

The Path of Unlight Barbarian is the worst of the three. It wants to get hit to trigger radiant retaliatory damage, but it comes with no way to taunt enemies to make that more likely to happen. What's worse, because this Barbarian automatically blasts light around itself like a flashlight, the class's level six blindsight ability is entirely useless unless you're using Darkness, which then makes enemies less likely to hit you.

Being lit up like a Christmas tree seems like a terrible survival strategy in the Underdark.

Most damning of all, the numbers seem completely wrong at higher levels. The Level 10 ability deals 1d6 damage per turn which doesn't scale, and at Level 14 you get a completely abysmal capstone, dishing out just 1d12 damage (and your enemies can make a save to halve this!) It's actually shocking that this made it into the world as is, even if it's only an Unearthed Arcana. Anyone with even a cursory knowledge of the game can see something ain't right here.

The House Agent Rogue is also anemic in combat. It gets some nice utility options, with manipulative spells like Suggestion and Charm Person, and the idea is that you're using Influence while in combat, which is really fun.

It all feels a bit janky though, like it doesn't quite hang together though. The backstab abilities require you to sacrifice too much damage to be more than situational, you don't get enough combat tricks before level nine, and are you really going to be able to persuade your enemies in the middle of a pitched battle? It gets good at level 17, when the campaign's probably almost over.

Finally, the Imaskarcanist Wizard has the worst name but better rules. It's a dabbliing healer, which isn't that great with the Wizard's low hit die, but it can also end harmful debuffs, which is truly useful. It also gets an incredibly fun capstone that turns an enemy into a glowing, ticking time bomb. I wish there was more stuff like that in here.

Overall, this is one of the worst UA Wizards of the Coat has put out in a long time, a real let down after the villainous subclasses we got in June. However, I have faith that in time these will turn out alright. There are the bones of some good ideas here, they've just gotten all jumbled up, and someone accidentally stuck a thumb spike on a nose.

At least you can turn into a Mind Flayer now!

title: Warhammer 40k's new Space Marine bike captain is SCREAMING White Scars
content:
On Monday, Games Workshop revealed a brand new Space Marine captain on bike model for Warhammer 40k, bringing back a classic commander that was demoted to Legends for the duration of 10th edition. It's good news for anybody who enjoys mounting their marines on coffin-shaped motorbikes and excellent news for White Scars players, who we can already hear breathing in so they can scream "For the Khan!" at the top of their lungs.

Shared on the Warhammer Community website on Monday, the kit in the marketing images might be painted in standard Ultramarines blue, but all the Space Marine chapters can take this guy. As befits a mighty hero of the Imperium his ride is tricked out with plenty of bling, and the model itself has several build options: three unhelmeted heads, two helmets, and a choice of power sword, thunder hammer, or plasma pistol for the captain's outstretched right hand.

GW has also revealed one of the rules for this version of the Captain: he gives the 40k ability Cleave 1 to the unit of Outriders that he leads, making them much more effective at carving a path through big blocks of infantry. If he were joining the game midway through an edition I'd compare him to the Chaplain on bike, but we know that the Space Marines are next up on the 40k Codex release schedule after the Orks, and so there's no telling what rules will change and what will stay the same.

The Captain will ride to war "at the same time as the upcoming Codex: Space Marines", alongside new multipart Space Marine Outrider models which were revealed in June. The question, of particular interest to White Scars player, is whether any other kits are going to be added to the motorpool?

If we go off what the Orks' range just received in the wake of its new Codex, almost all the new kits are resculpts of old models. I could see a revamp of the Invader ATV happening - the suspension on that ridiculous go-kart just makes me sad - but if GW plans to revamp kits from that era, the more prominent Intercessors, Aggressors, and Reivers are probably a higher priority.

What Space Marines models do you want to see get new kits? Share your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Brings Slavic & Balkan Folklore to Life in a New Fantasy TTRPG Setting
content:
Eren Chronicles has launched Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch, a new tabletop role-playing game setting inspired by Slavic and Balkan folklore, on Kickstarter. The campaign, which went live on Tuesday, has already surpassed $120,000 in funding within its first day, making it one of the most notable Dungeons & Dragons 5e campaigns of the year.

Zamanora transports players and Dungeon Masters into a world of rural communities, dark forests, and vengeful witches. The setting is designed to support both Wizards of the Coast’s Dungeons & Dragons 5e and 2024 editions, as well as Legend In The Mist, the rustic fantasy RPG from Son of Oak Game Studio that was recently voted the Most Anticipated TTRPG of 2025.

The Zamanora setting draws heavily from Slavic and Balkan folklore, offering players a chance to explore a world where cautionary tales come to life. Players can create characters from fantastical local creatures such as the mischievous Chorts and the spectral Huants. The setting also introduces unique subclasses, including the Bogatyr fighter, Guslar bard, and Hearth-domain cleric, allowing for thematic storytelling deeply tied to the region’s traditions.

Two new magic systems are introduced in Zamanora: Poppet Magic, a manipulative form of spellcasting, and Ceremonial Magic, which enables non-casters to perform magical rituals. These systems provide fresh ways for players to engage with the game world.

The setting features a variety of mythical creatures familiar to fans of Slavic and Balkan folklore, such as the leshy, baba yaga, and kikimora. These beings are joined by a host of other monsters, each accompanied by detailed descriptions and lore.

The Zamanora Kickstarter offers a range of rewards for backers, from digital PDFs to deluxe collector’s editions. Pledge tiers include options for digital content, physical books, and various accessories. The Core, Deluxe, and Collector’s Boxes include items such as dice, a GMless adventure deck, Baba Yaga miniatures, a DM screen, a monster deck, an illustrated slipcase, and a hand-knitted plushie.

A free demo of the Zamanora setting is available for download on the Kickstarter page, allowing potential backers to explore the world before committing to a pledge.

For more information or to support the project, visit the Zamanora: Ballad of the Witch Kickstarter page.

title: New Reinforcements Arrive in Infinity: PanOceania, Yu Jing, Shindenbutai, and Nomads Expand Their Forces
content:
Corvus Belli has introduced a series of new units and expansion packs for its tabletop game, Infinity, bringing additional options to the PanOceania, Yu Jing, and Shindenbutai factions, while also adding the Nomads to the mix.

Kestrel Expansion Pack Beta: PanOceania’s Colonial Forces

The Kestrel Colonial Force is featured in this expansion, showcasing PanOceania’s adaptability in addressing the challenges of space colonization. As a leading power in the Human Sphere, PanOceania leverages its resources to maintain its position, and the Kestrel forces exemplify this approach. Equipped with advanced technology, these units are designed to uphold PanOceania’s strategic interests.

White Banner Expansion Pack Beta: Yu Jing’s Strategic Elite

Yu Jing, often regarded as one of the top powers in the Human Sphere, continues to strengthen its military capabilities with the White Banner Army. This force has demonstrated its effectiveness in conflicts such as the struggle over Svalarheima. Combining cultural heritage with modern technology, the White Banner Army represents Yu Jing’s commitment to achieving its goals through disciplined and strategic action.

Shindenbutai Expansion Pack Beta: Tradition Meets Innovation

On the distant planet of Shinju, the Shindenbutai serve as the military arm of Greater Independent Japan. This force blends traditional samurai values with advanced technology, creating a unique and versatile unit. Tasked with protecting Japanese interests in Shinju’s challenging environment, the Shindenbutai offer players a distinctive option for their armies.

Yu Jing Action Pack and PanOceania Support Pack

The Yu Jing Action Pack provides players with additional units to enhance their armies, reflecting the faction’s combination of cultural depth and technological advancement. Meanwhile, the PanOceania Support Pack introduces specialized units such as the Trauma-Docs and Machinists, which focus on medical support and technical maintenance to keep PanOceanian forces operational.

JSA Support Pack: The Auxiliary Regiment

The Japanese Secessionist Army (JSA) gains new support options with the Tokusetsu Butai, or Auxiliary Regiment. This unit provides essential medical and technical services, ensuring that the JSA’s front-line forces remain effective. The pack highlights the JSA’s emphasis on a balanced approach to warfare, where support units play a critical role.

Nomads Action Pack: A Faction of Free Spirits

The Nomads, known for their independent and unconventional nature, join the battlefield with their own Action Pack. Originating from three massive spaceships that travel the Human Sphere, the Nomads challenge established norms and offer a unique playstyle. Their focus on creativity and adaptability makes them an appealing choice for players seeking a different approach to the game.

title: PAX East 2025 Tabletop Exhibitors Announced: Gloomhaven, Marvel’s Dice Throne, and More to Showcase in Boston
content:
The organizers of PAX East 2025, ReedPop and Penny Arcade, have revealed an initial look at the tabletop exhibitors set to appear at next year’s event. The East Coast’s largest gaming convention will return to the Boston Convention & Exhibition Center from May 8–11, 2025, featuring a dedicated section for tabletop gaming enthusiasts.

Among the exhibitors announced are the creators behind some of the industry’s most popular titles, including Gloomhaven from Cephalofair Games, Marvel’s Dice Throne from Dice Throne, and Settlers of CATAN from CATAN Studio. Other notable participants include UVS Games, known for Critical Role: Heroes of Exandria, and Chooseco, the publisher behind the iconic Choose Your Own Adventure gamebooks.

This initial announcement highlights just a portion of the over 110 exhibitors expected to attend. The full lineup will include a diverse range of tabletop and video game publishers and developers, with additional reveals planned throughout March and April. Attendees can also look forward to updates on the event’s content schedule, including the popular Storytime keynote, in the coming months.
